item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Ryan McMahon Trade Rumor Puts More Pressure on Brian Cashman to Find 3B Solution
item.dc:creator: Jovan Alford; Unknown
item.description: Earlier this week at the league’s annual GM Meetings in Las Vegas, Nevada, New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman told reporters that rebuilding the team’s bullpen is the club’s main priority. item.content:encoded:
Earlier this week at the league’s annual GM Meetings in Las Vegas, Nevada, New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman told reporters that rebuilding the team’s bullpen is the club’s main priority.
On paper, that makes sense since the team has several relievers hitting free agency, and isn’t guaranteed to get them all back. However, Yankees fans would also tell Cashman that third base should be a priority too, which was an albatross due to Ryan McMahon’s play on the field and at the plate.
The Yankees know third base is an issue, but deciding how to fix it isn’t simple. That said, New York is already taking the first step, and that’s to find a suitor for McMahon.
On Friday morning, Jon Heyman of the New York Post reported that the 32-year-old infielder is on the trade block. Heyman adds that for a deal to happen, the Yankees will “pay down his $16M salary or take a bad contract back.”
Ideally, the Yankees would pay down the salary rather than take a bad deal in a potential trade for McMahon. However, beggars can’t be choosers. It won’t be easy trying to find a suitor for the veteran. But with the free-agent market not overwhelmingly great at third base, it could work to the Yankees’ favor.
Yankees must do whatever it takes to find an upgrade at third base
That said, once the Yankees part ways with McMahon, they need to find a solution at the hot corner immediately.
One solution could be Alec Bohm, whom the Yankees are reportedly interested in. The free agent infielder can play third and first base and is coming off an up-and-down 2026 campaign with the Philadelphia Phillies.
As one could imagine, Bohm donning the pinstripes doesn’t inspire much confidence, even though he’d be a right-handed bat, which would balance New York’s left-handed-dominant lineup. In 2026, he hit .292 with seven home runs, 38 RBI, and a .816 OPS against southpaws.
However, he wasn’t great defensively, sporting a .966 fielding percentage, eight errors, and a -10 Defensive Runs Saved Above Average.
That said, if you ask Yankee fans who they really want at third base, they’d say Japanese star Teruaki Sato, who is coming off a Triple Crown season with the Hanshin Tigers. But as Jack Curry said on The Michael Kay Show last week, the Yankees “have some pause about his ability to be a third baseman at the major league level."
And on top of that, scouts told USA TODAY’s Bob Nightengale that Sato “will likely play the outfield if he signs with an MLB team” (h/t FOX Sports MLB). We can likely rule out Sato in the Big Apple.
Where does that ultimately leave the Yankees? The trade market. Do they pursue a trade for Isaac Paredes of the Houston Astros? He would be an ideal right-handed power bat, with 25 home runs and 94 RBI in 2026.
If not Paredes, would they go after Corey Seager of the Texas Rangers, which would require him to move to third base since the Yankees already have George Lombard Jr..
There are a lot of different avenues Cashman can go down to solve third base, but he needs to pick the right one because the Yankees can’t be in this spot again next year.
Jovan has over 13 years of experience in sports media, including stops at The Philadelphia Tribune, SB Nation, FanSided and Hoops Habit. Most recently joining OnSI, his teams covered include the New York Jets, New York Yankees and New York Knicks.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Jazz Chisholm Jr. or Brandon Lowe? Who Is a Better Fit for the Blue Jays?
item.dc:creator: Yirsandy Rodriguez; Unknown
item.description: At his best, Jazz Chisholm Jr. is a player who still retains several skills to impact the game, but the big problem throughout his career has been his constant performance decline. Leaving his controversies with the New York Yankees, Chisholm Jr. has reached free agency this year after a major decline compared to his 2025 season, when he recorded 4.3 fWAR, the highest figure of his career. The critical point that generated the most doubt for the Yankees was his decline in offensive production. J
item.content:encoded:
At his best, Jazz Chisholm Jr. is a player who still retains several skills to impact the game, but the big problem throughout his career has been his constant performance decline.
Leaving his controversies with the New York Yankees, Chisholm Jr. has reached free agency this year after a major decline compared to his 2025 season, when he recorded 4.3 fWAR, the highest figure of his career. The critical point that generated the most doubt for the Yankees was his decline in offensive production.
Jazz was basically the same hitter, prone to recording high rates of missed swings and strikeouts, capable of drawing walks consistently during his best stretches, with elite bat speed and a high rate of hard-hit balls. He also made greater use of his speed and set a personal record with 41 stolen bases, finishing in 10th place in the league with +5 Baserunning Runs. In addition, he was the second-most efficient baserunner in baseball at stealing third base this year.
However, the regression in his power gave his campaign a different turn. With 532 plate appearances, just one more than in 2025, Chisholm Jr. went from hitting 31 home runs and driving in 80 runs to recording 19 home runs and 55 RBIs, with the worst OPS (.589) and wRC+ (57) of his career with runners in scoring position in a single season. Overall, his xwOBA plummeted from .345 last year to .294, while his wRC+ fell from 125 to 98.
Chisholm Jr. vs. Lowe… Who Should Be Toronto’s Main Target?
Even in what was a year of regression in terms of production and impact compared to the expectations he left in 2025, Jazz remains an interesting player. He fell from the 85th percentile to the 22nd in Batting, but finished in the elite, at the 96th percentile in Base Running and the 86th in Fielding. So his numbers remain competitive, even though overall they fell short of Lowe’s great impact in 2026.
That said, if I had to choose the better version between Chisholm Jr. and Lowe as an option for the Jays, I would lean a little toward the former Yankee for a few obvious reasons. First of all, of course, he would become a division rival of the Yankees!
In addition, he would become an eye-catching piece to strengthen their archrivals, who eliminated them in the 2025 postseason. Can you imagine Jazz stepping up to the plate in the Bronx wearing the Blue Jays uniform? That would be fun to watch!
Look, both are power-hitting left-handed batters and, as I have written before, I also love Lowe, who is well known to the Yankees; he spent his first eight Major League seasons playing for the Tampa Bay Rays. But if Jazz bounces back and focuses more on how to make the most of his tools, he could be a more valuable player to contribute to Toronto’s lineup.
Lowe leads all Major League second basemen with 87 home runs over the last three seasons and is coming off his best offensive year, with personal records of 35 home runs and 4.9 fWAR. However, Jazz has also shown power, is a better baserunner and leads over that same period with 112 stolen bases.
In 2026, the Jays were the team that scored the fewest runs in all of Major League Baseball, with 648, and the fourth team with the fewest stolen bases, with 75. Jazz alone accounted for 54.6% of that figure with his 41 stolen bases and, if he manages to recover his power, I would not rule out that he could record his second 30-30 season.
Chisholm Jr. is also a more complete fielder at second base, with better range and a much more consistent track record than Lowe, who would still have to prove that his defensive improvements at second base can be repeated in 2027.
Yirsandy is a baseball writer specializing in MLB coverage with experience across multiple teams and storylines. He currently writes for Diamond Centric, where he covers the New York Mets, San Diego Padres, Chicago Cubs, Milwaukee Brewers, and Kansas City Royals. My work focuses on game coverage, player analysis, and storytelling that connects performance with context. My Substack has also been an important part of my writing development, where I’ve built much of my baseball coverage and storytelling voice over time. I’m passionate about combining reporting, research, and thoughtful analysis to produce engaging baseball content for readers.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees general manager Brian Cashman spent 75 minutes on Tuesday giving reporters his view of the team. He admitted the club has been good but not great for parts of the last two decades. The talk took place at the general managers' meetings in Las Vegas.
“We've been good but we haven't been great,” Cashman said, according to NJ.com. He did not pin the blame for the 2026 season on his players.
Three lineup roles remain unsettled: second base, third base, and designated hitter. The free agent market is only about two weeks old. Teams are still making offseason roster decisions.
In August, Yankee Global Enterprises announced a $2.6 billion financing agreement with Apollo Sports Capital, a combination of credit and equity. The Steinbrenner family retained full control of the Yankees.
Cashman said owner Hal Steinbrenner gave him a payroll limit. “I know what my limitations are … (Steinbrenner) told me he'd like me to stay under this number,” Cashman said.
The team recently parted ways with advisors Brian Sabean and Omar Minaya. “As costs continue to stretch here, I had some tough decisions to make,” Cashman said. “We're not going to replace or not going to duplicate those positions or replace them as we move forward.”
Cashman also spoke with former catcher Jorge Posada, who said he did not feel welcome at spring training. “If anybody has anything they want to add or question, my phone is available. We value our present, but we also value our past,” Cashman said.
Cashman tossed around a few what-if lineups. One had Ben Rice at first base and Luis Garcia at second. Rice finished last year with minus-9 Defensive Runs Saved and minus-4 Outs Above Average at first.
Garcia's numbers were worse. He ended 2025 with the Washington Nationals at minus-17 Defensive Runs Saved at second base, a mark that tied for the worst in both leagues. His Outs Above Average came in at zero. The Nationals also experimented with him at first base late in the season.
Cashman said Anthony Volpe's .245 average and career-low .336 slugging percentage “wasn't what we expected.” He added, “I think (Volpe) can be an average to above average player in the major leagues.” George Lombard Jr. is also in the infield mix.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers will almost certainly sign at least one relief pitcher this offseason.
Three of the Dodgers' biggest free agents — Evan Phillips, Alex Vesia and Blake Treinen — were relievers. Phillips has already signed with the Atlanta Braves on a three-year, $35 million deal, while Vesia is drawing interest from half the league and could be priced out of the Dodgers' range. As for Treinen, it's unclear if he'll be continuing his career heading into what would be his age-39 season.
The Dodgers could still retain Vesia or Treinen. If they don't, it's likely they'll sign at least one bullpen arm to fill the void left by the three pitchers — and they seem to be targeting one potential Vesia replacement.
Jon Heyman of the New York Post reported that the Dodgers are among the five teams interested in New York Yankees free agent left-handed reliever Tim Hill.
Heyman says the Yankees and Cleveland Guardians are "at the forefront" of the pursuit. Behind them are the Dodgers, New York Mets and San Francisco Giants.
How Would Tim Hill Fit With the Dodgers?
Hill, who turns 37 in February, is a nine-year MLB veteran who's been with the Yankees since June 2024.
The soft-tossing, sidewinder has a career 3.94 ERA over 519 appearances with the Kansas City Royals, San Diego Padres, Chicago White Sox and Yankees. Over the last three seasons in New York, he's accumulated a 3.34 ERA over 169.2 innings.
Hill is much more of a lefty specialist, as left-handed batters have a career .588 OPS against him. Right-handed hitters, on the other hand, have an .807 OPS.
That makes Hill not an exact replacement for Vesia, who's been fairly neutral against both righties and lefties in his career. Still, he would add a left-hander to a bullpen that's currently very right-handed heavy with the likes of Edwin Diaz, Edgardo Henriquez, Brock Stewart and Will Klein, among others.
The Dodgers don't appear to be the most aggressive players in the Hill sweepstakes. However, they'll likely add to the bullpen at some point, which general manager Brandon Gomes alluded to at this week's GM Meetings.
"Bullpen is probably an opportunistic thing, and looking at who fits within our group," Gomes said. "We have a lot of really young, talented guys that you could go out and give reps to and see who emerges. We didn’t expect Edgardo to be on the team coming out of the season, but he pitched himself into a high-leverage role. So it’s balancing that, making sure you have enough depth, but also some opportunity for young guys to really emerge."
Spotrac projects Hill's market value at one year and $5.6 million. In 2026, he earned $2.85 million.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Dodgers interested in former Yankees left-hander
item.dc:creator: Matt Borelli
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers saw several important players reach free agency at the start of the offseason, including Alex Vesia, who is arguably the top left-handed relief pitcher on the market. Vesia is reportedly drawing interest from multiple teams, and while the Dodgers would love to bring him back, a potential bidding war could lead to him signing a more lucrative contract elsewhere. Due to that uncertainty, the Dodgers could consider other options and are said to be among the teams interested
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers saw several important players reach free agency at the start of the offseason, including Alex Vesia, who is arguably the top left-handed relief pitcher on the market.
Vesia is reportedly drawing interest from multiple teams, and while the Dodgers would love to bring him back, a potential bidding war could lead to him signing a more lucrative contract elsewhere.
Due to that uncertainty, the Dodgers could consider other options and are said to be among the teams interested in signing Tim Hill, via Jon Heyman of the New York Post.
The Yankees are interested in bringing back Tim Hill. The Guardians, Mets, Giants and Dodgers are among other teams in the mix
— Jon Heyman (@JonHeyman) November 12, 2026
The Dodgers would presumably only put together an offer for Hill if they are unable to re-sign Vesia. But the 36-year-old also has plenty of suitors, so reaching a deal with either player is far from guaranteed.
Hill is coming off somewhat of a down season with the New York Yankees that saw him post a 5-2 record with a 4.60 ERA, 5.93 FIP and 1.14 WHIP in 58.2 innings across 67 appearances. Hill did limit left-handed batters to a .213/.265/.346 batting line with only seven extra-base hits in 137 plate appearances, showing he is still capable of being a solid situational reliever.
Prior to that, Hill had posted a much better 3.22 ERA in 132 combined games across the 2024 and 2025 seasons, so his recent track record is also appealing despite struggling a bit this year.
Interestingly, the Dodgers were linked to Hill two offseasons ago before he re-signed with the Yankees on a one-year contract that included a club option for 2026, so he is a player that the organization has liked in the past.
Whether that translates to a deal this time around remains to be seen, but Hill would be a good fallback plan in the event Vesia departs as a free agent.
Dodgers projected bullpen in 2027
As it currently stands, the Dodgers’ bullpen is set to return Edwin Díaz, Tanner Scott, Jack Dreyer, Edgardo Henriquez and Brock Stewart, among others, next season.
Scott and Dreyer are the only notable left-handers, depending on Justin Wrobleski’s role, so re-signing Vesia, adding Hill or acquiring another southpaw should be a priority for the Dodgers this offseason.

item.title: [The Times of India] How Alex Rodriguez transformed MLB fame into a business empire: What role do real estate, investments, business partnerships and luxury living play in building his estimated $350 million fortune in 2026
item.dc:creator: Global Sports Desk
item.description: Alex Rodriguez’s journey through the financial world is a textbook example of how success in professional sports can be the springboard to a broader business career. He played for the Seattle Mariners, Texas Rangers and New York Yankees for 22 seasons in MLB and earned more than $450 million in player salaries. His record-breaking contracts helped lay the financial groundwork for his off-the-field ventures. Celebrity Net Worth has updated its numbers, and as of 2026, Alex Rodriguez’s net worth i
item.content:encoded:
Alex Rodriguez’s journey through the financial world is a textbook example of how success in professional sports can be the springboard to a broader business career. He played for the Seattle Mariners, Texas Rangers and New York Yankees for 22 seasons in MLB and earned more than $450 million in player salaries. His record-breaking contracts helped lay the financial groundwork for his off-the-field ventures.
Celebrity Net Worth has updated its numbers, and as of 2026, Alex Rodriguez’s net worth is estimated to be about $550 million, or about $350 million. He has grown through his real estate holdings, business interests and ownership of sports franchises.
Inside Alex Rodriguez's wealth beyond his MLB career
Rodriguez started building his business portfolio while playing professional baseball, and he began investing in real estate in 1995, purchasing a duplex and adding more property to his portfolio. His approach early on was to build financial stability that extended beyond the limited duration of an athlete's playing career.
He later founded A-Rod Corp, a diversified investment firm that includes real estate, technology, sports, entertainment and consumer businesses. The company’s portfolio includes more than 40 companies and partnerships valued at more than $1 billion, according to the company’s official website.
Its real estate business has acquired more than $1 billion in assets and developed more than 15 million square feet of space.
How real estate and investments expanded Rodriguez's fortune
Real estate was one of Rodriguez's first and most important business interests. He also diversified into multifamily housing and property development throughout the U.S. with Monument Capital Management, which he co-founded with Ramon Corona.
He then expanded his investment portfolio beyond property into technology, wellness and consumer businesses. Through his A-Rod Corp, Rodriguez has invested in companies such as Vita Coco, Snapchat, Hims & Hers and Acorns, showing how Rodriguez has diversified his financial interests beyond his baseball earnings of the past.
Alex Rodriguez turned partnerships into business success
Business relationships also permitted Rodriguez to pursue his corporate ambitions. In 2021, he partnered with entrepreneur Marc Lore to create VCP Ventures. The two later partnered to buy the Minnesota Timberwolves and Minnesota Lynx.
Rodriguez became co-chairman of both teams when the NBA approved their buyout in June 2025. The partnership put him on top of sports ownership and gave him a reach beyond baseball.
How luxury living and sports ownership shape Rodriguez's lifestyle
Rodriguez’s financial success has also spilled over into his real estate selections and lifestyle. His property history includes luxury homes in Miami and the Hollywood Hills and high-profile purchases he made while dating Jennifer Lopez.
But luxury properties are just one aspect of his financial portfolio. His ties to the Timberwolves and Lynx have taken on added meaning since the franchise was reportedly valued at $4.5 billion in 2026. A revised valuation helped add to the updated valuation of Rodriguez’s fortune at $550 million, according to Celebrity Net Worth.
His role as an analyst for Fox Sports, his appearances on Shark Tank and other media endeavors have only added to his public profile. Rodriguez’s transition from MLB superstar to investor and sports executive demonstrates how career earnings, strategic alliances, and long-term investments can open doors well beyond the world of professional athletics.

item.title: [Pinstripe Alley] Yankees 2026 Roster Report Cards: Luis García Jr.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Diemert
item.description: It’s very tempting to want to love Luis García Jr. His lefty swing reminds me so much of Robinson Canó, and indeed my own swing is modeled after the former Yankee All-Star. At the time the Yankees dealt for him, desperate to get some kind of thump in an Aaron Judge-less lineup, he led the National League in slugging. When he came to New York, he clubbed a long home run in his second game, a worthy introduction to the Bronx faithful. After that, he was fine in the regular season, dreadful in Octo
item.content:encoded:
It’s very tempting to want to love Luis García Jr. His lefty swing reminds me so much of Robinson Canó, and indeed my own swing is modeled after the former Yankee All-Star. At the time the Yankees dealt for him, desperate to get some kind of thump in an Aaron Judge-less lineup, he led the National League in slugging. When he came to New York, he clubbed a long home run in his second game, a worthy introduction to the Bronx faithful. After that, he was fine in the regular season, dreadful in October, and now is the source of a bit of a logjam on the roster.
Grade: B-
2026 Stats (With Yankees): 43 G, 169 PA, 21 R, 42 H, 6 2B, 7 HR, 16 RBI, 1 SB, .264/.302/.434, 102 OPS+, 104 wRC+, 0.5 fWAR, 0.6 bWAR.
2027 Contract Status: Arb eligible
To Brian Cashman’s credit he made more than one deal for bats at the deadline, but neither Heliot Ramos nor García Jr. really had the impact I’m sure he planned. Luis came in in grand style:
Will forever love you, Ruocco.
That the Yankees went on to lose that game, one of the stupider of the year and what a list that makes, maybe says something about García Jr. as a Yankee. Getting him was the right move, it just never really paid off. I was surprised to see that he actually managed an 87 wRC+ in the postseason, because I genuinely would have thought he posted half of that.
To be fair, he was On One against the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, hitting .500, but then kind of everyone did that against the Red Sox in those two games. Facing the Rays in the ALDS Luis went 1-for-10, a -56 wRC+. The Yankees only who played three games against the Rays, if García Jr. went 1-for-10 in a random series in July we probably wouldn’t even notice, but it happened when the lights were brightest.
I’ve said this a lot about the 2026 Yankees, but Luis didn’t really do himself many favors. Yes, he has that big home run in his second game against the Cardinals, then he went two weeks without another dinger. He slugged .560 in Washington, .434 in New York. His strikeout rate jumped five points.
I do wonder how much the dimensions of Yankee Stadium worked against him. Luis was on pace for 33 doubles across 600 PA while with the Nationals, down to 22 over 600 PA in the Bronx. Yankee Stadium is a tremendous ballpark to hit home runs in, and not very friendly to other kinds of extra-base hits. The short right field wall was absolutely a reason why the club brought Heliot Ramos in, and maybe they believed that smooth lefty swing would turn some of those doubles into dingers for García Jr., but that didn’t happen, at least in 2026.
Moving into 2027, the Yankee have once again assembled a roster with so many first base/DH types. Giancarlo Stanton will be on the roster, Ben Rice is not going to be a catcher, Aaron Judge will almost certainly see less time in the outfield than we’re used to, if for no other reason than the game’s best hitter needs to sometimes be saved from himself. Then there’s García Jr., who on paper is possibly a better hitter than Stanton but not better than Rice or Judge, but also probably isn’t good enough at second base to merit uprooting Anthony Volpe.
Maybe that’s the project for this winter, making Luis García Jr. a functional second baseman and stick him in some kind of first base/second base platoon role. This gets complicated if there’s a lockout and teams can’t communicate with players, and is further complicated by the fact that the very bad Washington Nationals gave Luis 0 innings at the keystone last year.
I want to love Luis García Jr. I don’t think his performance in 2026 merits that love. I am hopeful, perhaps foolishly, that it will in 2027.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees pitching coach says quiet part out loud about Cam Schlittler's Cy Young season appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
New York Yankees pitching coach Matt Blake praised Cam Schlittler following the right-hander's unanimous American League Cy Young Award win.
Schlittler received the honor Wednesday after his first full major league season. The 25-year-old finished with an AL-leading 1.95 ERA and struck out 239 batters across 33 starts.
Speaking on MLB Network Radio on SiriusXM in a clip shared Thursday on X, formerly Twitter, Blake explained how Schlittler's 2026 campaign exemplified the aggressive approach he wants the Yankees' pitching staff to embrace.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"And you know, the big message for our whole group: just you know, you're not going to have as much margin for on the edges. Obviously, our catchers do a great job back there, but you know we've got to be more aggressive in the strike zone on the whole. And he's built to do that. You know he can live in the strike zone with his stuff."
He averaged nearly five strikeouts per walk, pairing swing-and-miss ability with limited free passes throughout his first full MLB campaign.
Schlittler went 14-6, issuing 49 walks over 193 2/3 innings. His combination of strikeouts and control accompanied one of the lowest qualifying ERAs in Yankees history.
Only Spud Chandler's 1.64 ERA in 1943 and Ron Guidry's 1.74 in 1978 rank lower among the franchise's qualifying starters.
Schlittler received all 30 first-place votes for 210 points. Toronto Blue Jays right-hander Dylan Cease finished second, followed by Cleveland Guardians left-hander Parker Messick.
The Massachusetts native became the Yankees' seventh Cy Young winner, joining Guidry and Gerrit Cole as the franchise's unanimous recipients.
New York selected Schlittler in the seventh round of the 2022 draft out of Northeastern. Four years later, he holds the American League's top pitching honor.
Schlittler's unanimous selection capped a breakout season that established him among MLB's premier pitchers.

item.content:encoded:
Ben Rice's breakout season with the New York Yankees has earned him another distinction, one that no other designated hitter in franchise history has achieved.
Rice was named to the All-MLB Second Team on Wednesday night, becoming the first Yankees DH to receive the honor since the awards were introduced in 2019.
The 27-year-old was recognized during the MLB Awards ceremony in Las Vegas, joining Houston Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez, who earned First Team honors at designated hitter.
Rice's selection capped an impressive season in which he established himself as one of baseball's most productive hitters, batting .264 with 41 home runs, 97 RBIs and an .897 OPS across 154 games.
The left-handed slugger ranked third in Major League Baseball in slugging percentage (.534) and fourth in OPS, while his 69 extra-base hits ranked sixth in the Majors.
He also finished with 16 game-winning RBIs, the fourth most in baseball.
Rice's power production placed him in rare company in Yankees history, joining Joe DiMaggio and Aaron Judge as the only players in franchise history to hit at least 40 home runs within their first three Major League seasons.
His 41 home runs represented a significant improvement over the 26 he hit in 2025, while his OPS increased from .836 to .897.
Rice also earned his first All-Star selection in July and participated in the Home Run Derby.
His success continued into October, when he hit four homers and drove in nine runs in five postseason games before the Yankees were eliminated in the American League Division Series.
A 12th-round selection out of Dartmouth College in the 2021 MLB Draft, Rice made his Major League debut in June 2024 and has developed into a middle-of-the-order power threat over the past three seasons.
Rice wasn't the only Yankees player recognized Wednesday.
Teammate Cam Schlittler earned First Team All-MLB honors after unanimously winning the American League Cy Young Award with a 14-6 record, 1.95 ERA and 239 strikeouts.

item.title: [New York Daily News] Yankees’ Brian Cashman spoke to Jorge Posada, Pat Murphy after viral comments
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips
item.description: Brian Cashman, speaking at the General Managers Meetings earlier this week, said that he and Jorge Posada have discussed the ex-catcher’s comments about not feeling wanted around the Yankees. “I don’t feel welcome when I go there,” Posada told “The Show,” in October when asked about potentially helping his former team. item.content:encoded:
Brian Cashman, speaking at the General Managers Meetings earlier this week, said that he and Jorge Posada have discussed the ex-catcher’s comments about not feeling wanted around the Yankees.
“I don’t feel welcome when I go there,” Posada told “The Show,” in October when asked about potentially helping his former team. While Posada acknowledged that he’s been a guest instructor in spring training, he added, “I don’t feel like they want me there, so I don’t go.”
On Tuesday, Cashman said that he was “surprised” by Posada’s comments. The general manager also mentioned that the four-time World Series champ, who played for the Yankees from 1995-2011, has been around in camp, and that he’s a regular at Old-Timers’ Day. Cashman even pointed out that Posada “did my daughter’s show,” a nod to the backstop’s appearance on the YES Network’s “Story of My Number,” hosted by Gracie Cashman.
“He is welcome,” the older Cashman said as part of a long response to Posada’s remarks. He made sure to tell Posada that during a recent phone call.
While Cashman was thrown off by Posada’s comments, there didn’t seem to be any hard feelings on his end. Cashman made it clear — amid a barrage of criticism from former Yankees and a 17-year title drought — that he and Hal Steinbrenner are always available if past pinstripers have thoughts or concerns.
“We’re not ducking calls or not taking calls or not having meetings or what have you. We value our present, but we also value our past,” Cashman said. “If any of our former guys want to engage, they know where to find us.”
He added that ridicule “comes with the territory” in a world oversaturated with content after Anthony Rizzo, CC Sabathia, Dellin Betances and Joe Girardi also questioned the Yankees’ culture and clubhouse following their ALDS loss to the Rays last month. Cashman previously said that he spoke to some other former Yankees after those comments were made, though he didn’t specify who.
Speaking specifically of Posada, Cashman said, “Jorge wants us to be great. We want us to be great. Unfortunately, we have been good, but we haven’t been great.”
Cashman noted that while Posada owns a few rings and an impressive résumé, “there were a lot of years he wasn’t able to push through [and win a championship] with his teammates.”
Cashman also addressed a viral moment in which Brewers manager Pat Murphy used some foul language to describe the Yankees after Milwaukee won the World Series. Murphy, having just beaten the Rays, was caught on a hot mic while celebrating with postseason standout and impending free agent Jake Bauers, who played on the 2023 Yankees club that didn’t make the playoffs.
“You’re going to be a rich motherf—,” Murphy told Bauers, “but just remember when you were on that horses— Yankees team and you guys were all playing for yourself. Just remember, say, ‘This is the way we used to do it.’”
Cashman said that Murphy called him less than 12 hours later to apologize. Considering Murphy was still flying high after winning the World Series, the gesture was appreciated by Cashman.
“[He was] explaining how he utilizes things, anything he can to motivate his players,” Cashman said. “But my biggest takeaway was that he took the time within 12 hours [of], arguably, some of the greatest times he’s had walking this planet earth, outside of the birth of his kids, to realize that he said something that he regretted that was caught on a live mic. And he wanted to take the time to track us down, the lowly New York Yankees, to make sure he had apologized for that. That meant a lot to me.”

item.content:encoded:
More than a third of MLB teams have spoken with Jazz Chisholm Jr. since the expiration of his previous contract with the New York Yankees, according to MLB Network's Jon Morosi.
Chisholm's representatives have spoken with 11 teams and scheduled "multiple in-person meetings" for next week, according to Morosi.
The Yankees declined to extend a qualifying offer to Chisholm after he slashed .231/.312/.399 in his second full season with the club.
Chisholm has already been connected to the Toronto Blue Jays, who Sportsnet's Shi Davidi reported met Wednesday with Chisholm's camp.
Blue Jays general manager Ross Atkins previously confirmed he plans to add to his offense this offseason, and Ernie Clement's position as the Blue Jays starting second baseman is in question heading into 2027, per MLB.com's Keegan Matheson.
According to Davidi, Chisholm also "is open to a versatile defensive role in which he moves between multiple positions, including the outfield."
MLB.com's Mark Feinsand previously named the Detroit Tigers, Los Angeles Angels, San Diego Padres and Cincinnati Reds as other potential landing spots for Chisholm.
Chisholm stole a career-high 41 bases while mostly playing second base this season but saw a drop in production from his 2025 All-Star campaign.
After posting a .242/.332/.481 slash line with 31 home runs and 31 stolen bases during his first full season since he was traded from the Miami Marlins, Chisholm avoided arbitration with the Yankees by agreeing to a $10.2 million salary ahead of the 2026 campaign.
He said shortly afterward he hoped to join the 50-50 club during his contract year, per MLB.com's Bryan Hoch.
Chisholm fell short of that goal this season and had a quiet playoffs, during which he batted .182 with zero RBI in four games before the Tampa Bay Rays swept the Yankees from the ALDS.
Whichever club signs Chisholm, potentially before the current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1, will hope a change of scenery and his reported willingness to switch defensive positions could help the two-time All-Star bounce back in 2027.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Rumor Suggests NY Yankees May Be Making Big Mistake By Letting Jazz Chisholm Leave in Free Agency
item.dc:creator: Jason Burgos

item.content:encoded:
While the large majority of New York Yankees fans welcome the idea of moving on from infielder Jazz Chisholm Jr., a new rumor may suggest that letting him walk in MLB free agency is a mistake.
There is no doubt that Chisholm Jr. has talent. He is a two-time All-Star who has a legit power bat and the rare skill set to be a 30-30 (home runs and stolen bases) player when he is hitting on all cylinders. Furthermore, he is a versatile fielder who can play multiple positions on the infield and outfield and is still in his 20s.
There is also no doubt that he can be a locker room problem. The Yankees knew that when they traded for him two years ago. But it was worth the risk because of his talent. However, his immaturity, lack of focus on defense, and a down season in 2026 have soured opinions about him among New York fans.
Yet, despite the obvious red flags in his character and baseball skills, it seems that Chisholm Jr. has fast become one of the most sought-after players in free agency. According to MLB Network's Jon Morosi, eleven teams are in discussions with Chisholm Jr.'s representatives, and "multiple in-person meetings are being scheduled next week."
If nearly a dozen teams are interested in the 28-year-old, are the Yankees making the wrong move by letting him walk?
Are the New York Yankees making a mistake by letting Jazz Chisholm walk?
If the Yankees let Chisholm Jr. leave, they have a hole at second base that won't be easily filled — whether you like him or not. While they have been linked to free agent second baseman Brandon Lowe, the word around the team is that they are more likely to address 2B internally with either Anthony Volpe or Luis Garcia Jr.
Volpe is not a problem child and is a solid player, but he can't create big moments like Chisholm Jr., and it is debatable whether he will be better defensively. Garcia Jr. is absolutely a better hitter, but there is a reason the Washington Nationals moved him from second to first base.
A case could certainly be made that, with a different manager or stronger leadership in the clubhouse, the negative parts of Chisholm Jr.'s personality could be held in check, so his positive energy and passion could be a huge plus for the team. Yet, neither is coming in 2027.
That is why the Yankees are not making a mistake by letting the infielder take his talents elsewhere. Nevertheless, it is still very interesting that so many teams want the player New York fans have grown tired of.

item.content:encoded:
SportsNet’s Shi Davidi reports that the Blue Jays “met Wednesday with representatives for Jazz Chisholm Jr.”

Meeting with representatives is standard practice for this time of year, but the Blue Jays seem keen to add offense to their infield mix, expressing an interest in Brandon Lowe and Ketel Marte as well. Perhaps the most significant development from the meeting with Chisholm is that the former Yankee is allegedly “open to a versatile defensive role in which he moves between multiple positions, including the outfield.” That would make Chisholm a better fit for the Blue Jays and other teams after he was used almost exclusively in the infield, mostly second base, by the New York Yankees over the past two-and-a-half seasons.

item.content:encoded:
Cam Schlittler, lanzador de los Yankees de Nueva York, ganó por unanimidad el premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana de 2026. Los 30 periodistas que votaron lo colocaron en primer lugar después de una temporada en la que lideró el circuito con 1.95 de efectividad, en su primera campaña completa en las Grandes Ligas.
El derecho de 25 años se convirtió en el séptimo pitcher de los Yankees en obtener el reconocimiento y el primero del equipo desde Gerrit Cole en 2023. Antes de él, los únicos Yankees que lo habían conseguido por unanimidad eran Cole en 2023 y Ron Guidry en 1978.
Los 30 votos dejaron a Schlittler por delante de Cease
La Asociación de Cronistas de Béisbol de Norteamérica (BBWAA) anunció el resultado el 11 de noviembre. Cada voto de primer lugar vale siete puntos, por lo que Schlittler obtuvo el máximo posible: 210.
Dylan Cease, de los Blue Jays de Toronto, terminó segundo con 110 puntos; Parker Messick, de los Guardians de Cleveland, quedó tercero con 84. Cease apareció en el segundo puesto de 22 papeletas y Messick ocupó esa posición en otras siete. Drew Rasmussen, de los Rays de Tampa Bay, recibió el voto restante para el segundo lugar y acabó cuarto.
La diferencia también se aprecia en los números de temporada regular. Cease igualó a Schlittler con 239 ponches, pero cerró con 2.40 de efectividad en 169 entradas, de acuerdo con los datos de los finalistas publicados por MLB. Schlittler trabajó 193 entradas y dos tercios y recibió 49 bases por bolas en 33 aperturas.
Una efectividad que lo acerca a la historia de los Yankees
Schlittler terminó la campaña con 14 victorias y seis derrotas. Sus 239 ponches empataron a Jack Chesbro en el cuarto total más alto para un lanzador de los Yankees en una temporada, según MLB.
Su efectividad de 1.95 fue la tercera más baja en la historia de la franquicia entre lanzadores calificados. Las únicas marcas inferiores fueron las de Spud Chandler, con 1.64 en 1943, y Guidry, con 1.74 en 1978. La efectividad mide el promedio de carreras limpias permitidas por cada nueve entradas lanzadas.
La constancia también acompañó ese promedio: permitió una carrera o menos en 21 de sus 33 aperturas, la mayor cantidad en las Grandes Ligas durante la temporada. Como visitante, registró 1.16 de efectividad en 17 salidas, de acuerdo con el recuento de MLB.
De las ligas menores al premio en dos temporadas
Los Yankees seleccionaron a Schlittler en la séptima ronda del draft de 2022, procedente de Northeastern University. Su ficha oficial de MLB sitúa su debut en las Grandes Ligas el 9 de julio de 2025. Ese año hizo 14 aperturas y terminó con 2.96 de efectividad.
El lanzador comenzó 2025 en la categoría Doble A. Al recordar su ascenso, dijo a MLB: "Me dieron una oportunidad y la aproveché".
En septiembre de 2026 volvió a enfrentar a Boston en el primer juego de la serie de comodín y lanzó seis entradas y un tercio sin permitir carreras. Ponchó a diez bateadores en la victoria 9-0 de los Yankees.
Esa actuación de postemporada quedó fuera de la evaluación del premio: la BBWAA recibe las papeletas antes de que comiencen los playoffs. La elección reconoció lo conseguido durante la temporada regular.
Los dos Cy Young fueron unánimes
En la Liga Nacional, Jacob Misiorowski, de los Brewers de Milwaukee, también recibió los 30 votos de primer lugar. Al igual que Schlittler, ganó el premio en su primera temporada completa en MLB.
La BBWAA señala que es apenas la tercera vez que los ganadores de ambas ligas son elegidos por unanimidad en un mismo año. Las anteriores fueron en 1968 y 2022. Misiorowski cerró su temporada después de ayudar a Milwaukee a conseguir su primera Serie Mundial.

item.title: [New York Post] Brian Cashman ‘not afraid’ to buck Yankees trend for David Bednar
item.dc:creator: Greg Joyce
item.description:
LAS VEGAS — Just because Brian Cashman has not dished out big bucks to a reliever since 2019 does not mean he is against doing so, according to the Yankees general manager. That may be put to the test in the coming weeks in the case of David Bednar.

item.content:encoded:
LAS VEGAS — Just because Brian Cashman has not dished out big bucks to a reliever since 2019 does not mean he is against doing so, according to the Yankees general manager.
That may be put to the test in the coming weeks in the case of David Bednar.




Access the Yankees beat like never before

Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
If the closer declines the $23.15 million qualifying offer that the Yankees extended to him by next Tuesday’s deadline (which appears more likely than not), Bednar will hit the open market primed for a payday as one of the top free-agent relievers.
And while there is nothing stopping the Yankees from negotiating a multi-year deal with Bednar before then – Cashman would not say if the two sides were talking about it – they may soon have to put their money where their mouth is in order to address one of their biggest needs this offseason.
“I’ve done it before, I’m not afraid to do it,” Cashman said at the GM meetings when asked about spending big on a reliever. “It just comes down to allocation of resources and the opportunity, what’s in front of you and how realistic it is, and do we like it enough to play those numbers and all that stuff. But I’m not opposed to putting numbers on players at whatever position.”
The Yankees have not put the kind of numbers that Bednar will get on a reliever since 2019, when they signed Zack Britton to a three-year, $39 million deal and added an extra year and $18 million to the five-year, $86 million pact Aroldis Chapman signed ahead of the 2017 campaign.
Neither deal ended well for the Yankees.
This time around, Cashman has said he is working under a budget from Hal Steinbrenner that he would not define.
But if the Yankees were able to offer Bednar the $23.15 million for one year (which would be the highest average annual value for any reliever), conceivably they should be able to fit in a multiyear deal, given that the AAV would likely be lower.
Former Yankees closer Devin Williams got three years and $51 million from the Mets last winter, which would seem to be in the neighborhood of what Bednar could land in free agency this offseason.
That the Yankees already know he can handle the bright lights of New York should make them more comfortable handing out that kind of money to a 32-year-old reliever.
“Listen, we dropped a big qualifying number on him — that factored [in] a lot,” Cashman said. “He’s a cool customer. From what I understand, even though I’m not in the bullpen, obviously, from what I hear from everybody involved — we’ve been very lucky over the course of time for the most part to have somebody with a strong presence and great leadership to lead out there, and he checked all those boxes along with the performance.
“So I’ve had some good additions, I’ve had some not-so-good additions. He’s been a good addition so far, and hopefully we find a way to keep him so I can worry about surrounding him with more quality individuals that our manager can turn to late in the game to try to close things out.”
Since Chapman and Britton left, the Yankees have either traded for established closers (Bednar, Williams) or found them through reclamation projects (Clay Holmes, Luke Weaver).
They may not have the luxury to try the latter at this point, given that lefty setup man Brent Headrick is the only full-time member of the 2026 bullpen guaranteed to return in 2027.
The other top reliever on the market is former Padres lefty Adrian Morejon, but he figures to be more expensive than Bednar and would also cost the Yankees draft-pick compensation and international bonus pool money because of the qualifying offer attached to him.
“[The bullpen] is probably our biggest need because we have so [many] vacancies of certainly important people that did a great job for us,” Cashman said, with Tim Hill and Paul Blackburn both free agents, while Fernando Cruz is trying to pitch through a partially torn UCL.
“Doesn’t mean we don’t have answers from within that can handle it somehow, some way. But you’re always wondering. You don’t know. There’s no certainty until you play it out and let it play out. So if I can pull down via trade or free agency some individuals that make you sleep better at night, even though bullpens are volatile regardless, that would be a priority for me.”

item.dc:creator: Greg Joyce
item.description:
LAS VEGAS — Those who wanted a shake-up on Aaron Boone’s coaching staff are getting it after all. The Yankees will have a new bench coach and hitting coach in 2027, after Brad Ausmus was named Astros manager Wednesday and James Rowson is set to become Giants offensive coordinator.

item.content:encoded:
LAS VEGAS — Those who wanted a shake-up on Aaron Boone’s coaching staff are getting it after all.
The Yankees will have a new bench coach and hitting coach in 2027, after Brad Ausmus was named Astros manager Wednesday and James Rowson is set to become Giants offensive coordinator.




Access the Yankees beat like never before

Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
Both men were on expiring contracts, having spent the last three seasons in The Bronx, but Rowson’s job appeared to be in greater danger after Hal Steinbrenner blamed the offense for another disappointing season that ended with a whimper in the ALDS.
One of the candidates to replace Rowson that the Yankees have spoken with multiple times is former Dodgers co-hitting coach Aaron Bates, a source said Wednesday. Bates had been on the Dodgers staff since 2019 before leaving last week when they were not able to agree on a new contract.
To replace Ausmus, the Yankees could turn to the man he is replacing in Houston. Joe Espada, who spent the past three years as the Astros manager and previously spent time in the Yankees organization, is among the candidates the Yankees will consider for their next bench coach, according to a source. Espada was a special adviser to Cashman before serving as Yankees third base/infield coach from 2015-17, then joined the Astros in 2018 as their bench coach.
“I think Joe’s a great baseball guy, but there’s a whole bunch of guys we’re going to have to sift through,” Cashman said. “So I think we’re all collectively putting names together. We’ll work through it with Booney and start interviews, but not this week.”
Ausmus and Rowson (who ran spring training together) joined major league field coordinator/director of catching Tanner Swanson, who was named Mariners bench coach, as departures from Boone’s staff this offseason. The Yankees have already promoted run prevention and catching coordinator Aaron Gershenfeld to take Swanson’s spot.
“Our coaching staff has been trying to get raided this winter,” Cashman said, offering it as proof that the Yankees are doing the right things.
Now, they will have to fill the bench coach and at least lead hitting coach vacancies at a time when Boone is entering the final year of his contract. Whether Boone’s lame-duck status will affect the pool of candidates they pick from to make those hires — potentially fearing that the Yankees could clean house if they do not win a championship in 2027 — remains to be seen.
Cashman said the Yankees would love to have a bench coach in place before the lockout begins at midnight Dec. 1, but does not want to rush through that decision and make the wrong choice. Hiring a new hitting coach (and possibly his new assistants) before then would be even more important, so he could connect with players before communication is forbidden during the lockout.
Rowson had been the Yankees hitting coach since 2024, after they fired Dillon Lawson midseason in 2023 and used Sean Casey as an interim hitting coach for the rest of that season. The Mount Vernon native, who previously spent time as the Yankees minor league hitting coordinator before working with the Cubs, Twins, Marlins and Tigers, had plenty of fans in the clubhouse, most notably Aaron Judge.
It is not yet clear what will happen with assistant hitting coaches Casey Dykes (who has been on the staff since 2022) and Jake Hirst (hired last offseason), who were both products of their minor league system.
Ausmus, meanwhile, had interviewed for both the GM and manager jobs with the Astros, the team he spent 10 seasons with as a catcher. The GM job ultimately went to Randy Flores before the Astros landed on Ausmus to succeed Espada.
As for the rest of Boone’s staff, pitching coach Matt Blake, assistant pitching coach Desi Druschel, bullpen coach Preston Claiborne, third base coach Luis Rojas and first base coach Dan Fiorito are all set to return.

item.content:encoded:
Grandes Ligas
Brian Cashman acepta las disculpas de Pat Murphy
El dirigente de los Cerveceros de Milwaukee, tras ganar la Serie Mundial, dijo que los Yankees de 2023 tenían una cultura egoísta
LAS VEGAS. — El gerente general de los Yankees, Brian Cashman, aceptó las disculpas de Pat Murphy después de que el mánager de Milwaukee criticara al equipo de Nueva York de 2023 por una cultura egoísta minutos después de que los Cerveceros ganaran la Serie Mundial el mes pasado.
Cuando el primera base Jake Bauers le entregó la pelota a Murphy en el último out del quinto partido contra Tampa Bay el 28 de octubre , el mánager usó una palabrota al referirse a los Yankees.
Murphy hizo referencia al probable contrato millonario de Bauers como agente libre esta temporada baja y le imploró que recordara su época en los Yankees de 2023, que terminaron con un récord de 82-80 y no lograron clasificar para los playoffs, y que la comparara con su éxito este año.
“Todos ustedes jugaban para sí mismos. Solo recuerden, digan: ‘Así es como solíamos hacerlo’”, dijo Murphy durante la celebración en el campo, un comentario que quedó registrado en un video publicado por Spectrum News 1 Wisconsin .
“Se tomó el tiempo, en uno de los momentos más importantes de su vida —en apenas 12 horas, posiblemente uno de los mejores momentos que ha vivido en este planeta, exceptuando el nacimiento de sus hijos—, para darse cuenta de que había dicho algo de lo que se arrepentía, algo que quedó grabado en directo”, dijo Cashman el martes en la reunión de gerentes generales. “Quiso tomarse el tiempo, buscarnos aquí en los modestos Yankees de Nueva York para asegurarse de disculparse por ello, así que eso significó mucho para mí”.
Cashman dijo que Murphy explicó "cómo utiliza las cosas, todo lo que está a su alcance, para motivar a sus jugadores".
Murphy ganó el premio al Manager del Año de la Liga Nacional el martes por la noche, convirtiéndose en el primer entrenador de cualquiera de las dos ligas en obtener este galardón tres temporadas seguidas. Comentó que Cashman fue muy amable y atento durante su conversación.
“No me refería específicamente a los Yankees”, dijo Murphy. “Era como un equipo de un gran mercado que firma muchos contratos a largo plazo con jugadores consagrados... Podría haber mencionado a cualquiera. Podría haber dicho los Dodgers, los Giants o quien fuera”.
Nueva York fue barrido por Tampa Bay en una Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana y no ha ganado la Serie Mundial desde su 26º título en 2009 .
“Los Marlins nos ganaron en la Serie Mundial y recuerdo que pusieron nuestro logo en el anillo de la Serie Mundial, que fue cuando vencieron a los Yankees”, dijo Cashman. “Tenemos una historia de éxitos a la que siempre intentamos estar a la altura”.
Cashman dijo que entiende el enfado de la afición del equipo al final de cada temporada sin un título.
“¿Me enfado? Al principio, sí. ¿Me motivo? Por supuesto, siempre”, dijo, rodeado de periodistas. “No necesito nada que me motive. Siento que nuestros fans, ustedes y ustedes, nos mantienen suficientemente motivados. Si eso no fuera suficiente, bueno, tendríamos una picana eléctrica constantemente conectada justo donde menos la queremos, con electrodos funcionando sin parar. Eso nos mantiene con vida. Pero también, cuando uno se detiene a reflexionar, tiene que canalizar y reconocer que todo proviene de la esperanza y el amor, del deseo de que las cosas mejoren”.
Cashman, que inicia su trigésima temporada al frente de las operaciones de béisbol de los Yankees, dijo que su nuevo contrato ya estaba finalizado, pero no reveló su duración.
“Aunque ya hemos pasado por esto antes, no ha sido tan oportuno como debería, así que lo entiendo”, dijo refiriéndose a la sequía de títulos. “Y cuanto más se prolonga, más se hace sentir la presión”.
Fried se somete a una cirugía de codo.
El lanzador zurdo de los Yankees, Max Fried, fue operado para extirparle un espolón óseo del codo con el que lanza.
“Fue una cirugía de última hora”, dijo Cashman. “Seis semanas de descanso y rehabilitación, y luego un programa de lanzamiento que comenzará, creo, la segunda semana de diciembre. Debería estar listo para los entrenamientos de primavera”.
Fried, tres veces All-Star y que cumplirá 33 años en enero, tenía un récord de 5-5 con una efectividad de 2.80 en 20 aperturas. Debido a lo que el equipo describió como una contusión ósea en el codo izquierdo, no lanzó para los Yankees entre el 15 de mayo y el 22 de julio, ni entre el 13 y el 29 de agosto.
Cashman habla con Posada
Cashman dijo estar sorprendido de que el ex receptor All-Star Jorge Posada dijera en un podcast con reporteros del New York Post que el equipo lo hizo sentir incómodo.
“Si alguno de nuestros exjugadores quiere hablar con nosotros, sabe dónde encontrarlos”, dijo Cashman. “Es bienvenido. Obviamente, hablé con él al respecto. ... Jorge quiere que seamos grandes. Nosotros también queremos ser grandes. Y, lamentablemente, no lo hemos sido; hemos sido buenos, pero no hemos sido grandes”.

item.content:encoded:
The mandate in the Bronx is unmistakable: bounce back in 2027. Following a deflating conclusion to the 2026 campaign—marred by untimely injuries to core stars Aaron Judge and Max Fried—the New York Yankees have turned their attention toward recalibration, with General Manager Brian Cashman addressing Judge’s durability and future deployment.
“I’m sure he’s going to need some DH time. I’m sure he doesn’t want to hear that. He’s an alpha, wants to play every day,” Cashman said of the captain, whose late-season injury cost him nearly the entire postseason.
While the front office evaluates external reinforcements—including reported interest in Japanese standout Shoki Oda—ensuring Judge returns at peak physical condition remains the club’s primary offseason objective.
Between potential roster turnover, including speculation surrounding infielder Ryan McMahon, manager Aaron Boone and the front office face a pivotal winter tasked with reconstructing a roster capable of snapping New York’s championship drought.
"I'm sure he's going to need some DH times. I'm sure he doesn't want to hear that. He's an alpha, wants to play every day"
Brian Cashman was asked if he thinks Aaron Judge will need to have some DH time to stay healthy going forward: pic.twitter.com/achqXh0muE
— SNY Yankees (@snyyankees) November 10, 2026
What happened to Aaron Judge?
On September 16 against the Minnesota Twins, Judge suffered a moderate-grade right calf (soleus) strain shortly after returning from a rib stress fracture, instantly casting a shadow over his postseason availability.
Brief public tension followed when Boone expressed skepticism regarding Judge’s timetable for the AL Wild Card Series, even as the slugger targeted a quick return. The severity of the strain won out, ultimately sidelining him for both the Wild Card round and the ALDS.
Judge avoided surgery and was cleared for full baseball activities ahead of spring training, though the Yankees intend to deploy him more frequently at designated hitter to safeguard his long-term health.
Key takeaways
- Brian Cashman addressed Aaron Judge’s durability and future designated hitter deployment for 2027.
- The New York Yankees reportedly showed interest in Japanese pitching standout Shoki Oda.
- Aaron Judge suffered a right calf strain on September 16 against Minnesota.

item.title: [New York Daily News] Yankees takeaways: Brian Cashman ‘not afraid’ to spend on bullpen, ‘open-minded’ at third base
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips
item.description: LAS VEGAS — With the GM Meetings in full swing and Major League Baseball speeding toward a lockout, Brian Cashman discussed the Yankees’ various needs on Tuesday. The CVS receipt-length list will require an abundance of resources, whether that be through free agency or trades. item.content:encoded:
LAS VEGAS — With the GM Meetings in full swing and Major League Baseball speeding toward a lockout, Brian Cashman discussed the Yankees’ various needs on Tuesday.
The CVS receipt-length list will require an abundance of resources, whether that be through free agency or trades. Cashman said that owner Hal Steinbrenner has given him a budget to work with, though the general manager declined to talk about the financial parameters he’s operating under after the Yankees spent a projected $341.8 million on their competitive balance tax payroll in 2026.
“It’s not in my interest to say,” Cashman said. “I just know what my limitations are.”
Cashman added that he is “approaching business as usual” with MLB owners and players fighting over the implementation of a salary cap. He has a lot of business to tend to with the current Collective Bargaining Agreement set to expire at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1. At that point, there will be a freeze on big league transactions until a new CBA is ratified.
It’s anyone’s guess when that will be.
With that in mind and a truncated offseason already underway, here’s what Cashman had to say about some of the Yankees’ most pressing roster questions.
‘NOT AFRAID’ TO SPEND ON PEN
The Yankees have not given big money to a free agent reliever since Zack Britton ($39 million) and Adam Ottavino ($27 million) signed three-year contracts in January 2019. Aroldis Chapman also signed a hefty extension with the team in November 2019.
Since then, the Yankees’ biggest multi-year contracts for free agent relievers have gone to Justin Wilson (2 years, $5.5 million) and Tommy Kahnle (2 years, $11.5 million). Meanwhile, they haven’t paid a reliever more than the $9 million David Bednar made in 2026 during that span.
Now Bednar is a free agent and weighing the one-year, $23.15 qualifying offer from the Yankees. He has until Nov. 17 to accept or reject it. Of course, he can also pursue a multi-year deal before and after that deadline.
While Cashman wouldn’t say if talks are ongoing with the closer, he did say “hopefully we find a way to keep him.” Cashman also said that the Yankees’ bullpen is a “priority,” as Brent Headrick is the only under-contract healthy reliever who spent the entire 2026 season with the big league club.
“I’ve done it before,” Cashman said when asked if he’s willing to spend big on multiple relievers. “I’m not afraid to do it. It just comes down to allocation of resources and the opportunity, what’s in front of you and how realistic it is and do we like it enough to pay those numbers and all that stuff. But I’m not opposed to putting numbers on players at whatever position.”
In addition to Bednar, the Yankees would also like to keep Paul Blackburn and have some interest in bringing back depth pieces like Tim Hill and Ryan Yarbrough. Adrian Morejon, another big-ticket item, Alex Vesia and JoJo Romero are some external names to watch.
MOVE ON FROM MCMAHON?
While Cashman believes that Ryan McMahon is capable of exceeding the minimal production he provided in 2026, the GM said that he’ll look to improve at third base “without a doubt.”
“He’s signed through next year for us, but I definitely know we need to improve production in a lot of different spots on the club if we can,” Cashman said. “So we’ll be open-minded to finding what we can run into if it’s there.”
As Cashman alluded to, McMahon is owed $16 million next season. And yet, the Yankees could cut bait after McMahon’s once-elite defense regressed while he continued to flop at the plate in 2026.
The Yankees don’t have great internal alternatives at third, with the light-hitting Anthony Volpe and José Caballero among them. The free agent market is also thin on options — there are questions about Japanese star Teruaki Sato’s defense — so the Yanks may have to pursue a trade at the hot corner. Houston could move Isaac Paredes, but his defense isn’t great either.
‘COMFORTABLE’ WITH INTERNAL OPTIONS AT SECOND
While Cashman said that he’s “a fan” of Jazz Chisholm Jr., it would be surprising to see the free agent return after a tumultuous, down year. Once again, that leaves Volpe and Caballero among the incumbent options at second base.
Cashman mentioned that he liked the way that Volpe, the Yankees’ former starting shortstop, transitioned to second this year, and that he still believes the career below-average hitter has more to offer offensively.
“We do have internal options that I’d say that we’re comfortable with,” Cashman said, “but at the same time, it’s my job to explore any outside opportunities that may exist as well.”
Regarding Volpe, Cashman added, “He’s put himself in the position for consideration and competition.”
Cashman also said that he spoke to Luis García Jr.’s agent about the first baseman working at second base — not third — this offseason, possibly while playing winter ball. García played second for the Nationals in 2025, but he was terrible amid some communication issues with the club’s coaching staff at the time.
THE 1B/DH LOGJAM
If García can play second adequately, it would unclog the Yankees’ logjam of first base/DH types.
With Giancarlo Stanton hurt all year, Ben Rice almost only DH’d after García was acquired from Washington over the summer. But Cashman said that the non-fielding Stanton will “absolutely” be with the Yankees in spring training; they’re giving the respected veteran a chance to show he’s healthy despite him suffering three calf strains in 2026 and his contract being in a place where the Yankees could stomach parting ways.
Rice, meanwhile, has become a “transformational player” and needs to be in the lineup every day, Cashman said. García is a slugger in his own right, though better against righties.
If García does play second, the Yankees will want to see improved defense from Rice at first.
Cashman also said that he’s “sure” that Aaron Judge is going to need more DH days after an injury-riddled season.
“I’m sure he doesn’t want to hear that, but he’s an alpha,” Cashman said. “I would think at times we’ll see Judge playing DH because it’s what’s in his best interest, and what’s in his best interest is going to be what’s in our best interest.”
IS JONES THE CENTER FIELDER?
With Trent Grisham another free agent who is not expected back, center field is also a question mark. Cashman said that Spencer Jones, a rookie in 2026, is “capable” of playing the position, but he looked shaky there and “probably profiles better on the corner.”
In a follow-up, Cashman said he’d be comfortable with Cody Bellinger as a full-time center fielder. He just won the Platinum Glove for his left field defense, but he hasn’t always graded out well in center.
Of course, the Yankees can also be “opportunistic in the marketplace” as they search for answers in center, Cashman said.
STILL LOOKING FOR A RIGHT-HANDED CATCHER
The Yankees have been looking for a right-handed hitting catcher to pair with the left-handed Austin Wells for some time. That search will continue this offseason, as Cashman acknowledged that Ali Sánchez, the right-handed hitting catcher that the team defaulted to in 2026, isn’t sufficient.
“The bat’s not a strong [calling] card for him,” Cashman said after complimenting Sánchez’s defense. “So if we can find a good defending, right-handed hitting option to level up, that’d be great. But that’s also slim pickings.”
FRIED HAD SURGERY
While the Yankees could trade from their surplus of starting pitching, Cashman did share that Max Fried recently underwent a procedure to remove a bone spur from his left elbow. Fried went on the injured list with a left elbow bone bruise twice in 2026.
The southpaw is now in the midst of a six-week shutdown from throwing. Cashman expects Fried to begin his throwing program around the second week of December. “He should be ready for spring training,” Cashman added, but who knows when that will begin.
Cashman also said that Judge had a follow-up consultation on his fractured rib with Dr. Gregory Pearl.
“He’s currently in a good place,” Cashman said, noting that “there’s no new procedures or anything there with Aaron Judge.”

item.content:encoded:
Yankees GM Brian Cashman acknowledged that Aaron Judge will probably need more DH days going forward.

Judge was limited to 66 games last season, is losing range in right field and is turning 35 in April, so, yeah, it’s probably time for the Yankees to start DHing him at least once a week or so. The Yankees are looking at getting Giancarlo Stanton back next season, but it’s hard to pencil him in at this point. They finished last season with Luis García Jr. at first base and Ben Rice at DH against righties. If Stanton is out of the picture, they could go with Judge at DH and Heliot Ramos in right field versus lefties next year.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Brian Cashman Reveals Terrifying Truth About Ben Rice’s Defense
item.dc:creator: Joey Haverford
item.description: The New York Yankees are trying to configure a roster with many defensive flaws next season, and Ben Rice may have the toughest job. MLB fans witnessed Rice emerging into one of the elite hitters of last season, but he couldn't play defense. Lackluster defensive skills saw the Yankees having Rice as the primary DH. Injuries to Giancarlo Stanton and Aaron Judge made it easier for Rice to avoid playing defense. However, Yankees GM Brian Cashman confirmed that will change. The media asked about Ric
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are trying to configure a roster with many defensive flaws next season, and Ben Rice may have the toughest job. MLB fans witnessed Rice emerging into one of the elite hitters of last season, but he couldn't play defense. Lackluster defensive skills saw the Yankees having Rice as the primary DH. Injuries to Giancarlo Stanton and Aaron Judge made it easier for Rice to avoid playing defense.
However, Yankees GM Brian Cashman confirmed that will change. The media asked about Rice's defense and Cashman provided a bold quote:
"It's just the way it is. I have no problem if Stanton is healthy and in the DH spot. It's not even an afterthought at this stage that Rice is playing first base for us. He's a given. I don't care if he's a 55 over there or a 45 defensively. I don't even worry about it."
The entire comment focused on wanting to get Stanton at bats at DH and Aaron Judge spending some time there. Cashman confirmed these variables will make Rice the everyday first baseman regardless of what his defense looks like. A full offseason could see Rice improving by spring training, but the risk is there for mistakes to haunt the team next year.
Why Yankees Fans Fear This Ben Rice Comment
Cashman's quote ended with him flat out saying he doesn't care or worry about any defensive woes from Rice. Luis Garcia is expected to move from first to second base to create two potential new flaws in an already limited defense.
The past few seasons have seen the Yankees developing a reputation for being a bad defensive team. Game 2 of the 2026 ALDS featured errors costing the Yankees their best chance to win a game against the Tampa Bay Rays and steal home field advantage.
An infamous World Series against the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2024 saw this becoming a huge issue to Yankees fans. The team fails to excel at the fundamentals and gives opponents more chances with weaker defense. Rice at first base could make this far worse since he'll be involved in every single ground ball defensive play as a flawed defender.
Understanding Brian Cashman's Bigger Point
The Yankees can't risk putting Rice at DH, so it isn't that Cashman is wrong in his thinking. Fans just hate seeing a glaring issue continue to get worse, especially since the offense has struggled compared to pitching.
The second base role will likely see both Anthony Volpe and Garcia splitting time there, despite neither man viewing that as their natural position. George Lombard was also the worst defensive shortstop in the league once he got called up last season.
Cashman is aware that the offense badly needs Judge to stay healthy and for Stanton to get at bats to help the team. Rice playing first base is the only answer to this issue, but any GM saying they don't care about bad defense is a terrible look. Aaron Boone will have a challenging job next season getting by with a potentially terrible defensive infield.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Brian Cashman Reveals Terrifying Truth About Ben Rice's Defense appeared first on HEAVY.

LAS VEGAS — After a season plagued by elbow issues, Max Fried has gotten an offseason cleanup.
The left-hander underwent surgery to remove a bone spur from his left elbow, Brian Cashman said Tuesday, though it should not affect his readiness for the 2027 season — whenever it actually begins, with a lockout looming.
Access the Yankees beat like never before
Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
The procedure — which was not originally on the docket when Cashman and Aaron Boone last spoke to reporters in late October — comes with six weeks of rest and rehab before Fried can begin a throwing program around the second week of December.
“He should be ready for spring training,” Cashman said during the general managers meetings at the Aria Resort and Casino.
In the 20 starts he did make, he was mostly terrific, pitching to a 2.80 ERA across 112 ²/₃ innings.
Aaron Judge recently had a follow-up appointment with Dr. Gregory Pearl — the specialist with whom the Yankees consulted on theircaptain’s broken rib last season — which essentially cleared him moving forward.
“He’s currently in a good place,” Cashman said. “So no new added features to his circumstance outside of, take the winter to continue to rest up and he’ll be ready to go. But there’s no new procedures or anything there with Aaron Judge.”
While pitching coach Matt Blake’s contract extension was previously reported, Cashman revealed that assistant pitching coach Desi Druschel and bullpen coach Preston Claiborne are also coming back, as are third base coach Luis Rojas and first base coach Dan Fiorito.
Bench coach Brad Ausmus, meanwhile, is still waiting to hear back from the Astros after he interviewed for both their GM job (which went to Randy Flores) and manager job (which remains open).
Go beyond the box score with the Bombers
Sign up for Inside the Yankees by Greg Joyce, exclusively on Sports+.
Thank you
Cashman on the Yankees not renewing the contracts of special advisers and former GMs Brian Sabean and Omar Minaya: “I was thankful that ownership allowed me to onboard those guys four years ago. As costs continue to stretch here, I had to make some tough decisions. We’re not going to replace or not going to duplicate those positions or replace them as we move forward. Unfortunately, there was some give that had to take place. They’re really excellent baseball people that I think will add value somewhere if somebody’s got an opportunity.”
