item.content:encoded:
Hideki Matsui is heading back to the most iconic franchise in Japanese baseball, and the move is giving collectors a new reason to revisit one of the hobby’s most important modern international careers.
The Yomiuri Giants introduced Matsui as their new manager on October 23, placing one of the most accomplished stars in Japanese baseball history back at the center of the team where he first became a national sensation. For collectors, the news does more than reconnect Matsui to the Giants. It adds another layer of historical meaning to his rookie cards, home run commemoratives, and Giants-era collectibles.
Matsui’s playing career already carried major hobby relevance on both sides of the Pacific. He was a slugging superstar for Yomiuri before becoming a marquee MLB name with the New York Yankees and later playing for the Angels, A’s, and Rays. Now, with a return to the Giants in a leadership role, his cardboard legacy gains another chapter tied directly to the club that first made him famous.
Why Matsui’s Return Matters to Collectors
The Yomiuri Giants are not just another team in Nippon Professional Baseball. They are one of the most recognized and most scrutinized organizations in Japan, with a national fan base and a history that reaches deep into the culture of the sport. Managing the Giants is widely viewed as one of the highest-profile jobs in Japanese sports, which means Matsui’s appointment immediately carries weight far beyond a standard coaching change.
For more collector background, read Top 3 Gale Sayers Cards Ever: His Most Valuable and Iconic Football Issues.
That prominence matters in the hobby. Collectors often place additional value on cards when a player’s legacy expands beyond playing accomplishments alone. Hall of Fame elections, milestone anniversaries, championships, awards, and managerial appointments can all shift how collectors view an athlete’s career arc. Matsui’s return to Yomiuri fits that pattern because it connects his playing days, his cultural importance, and the legacy of the Giants in a single storyline.
For longtime collectors of Japanese baseball cards, Matsui already stood as one of the cornerstone names of the 1990s and early 2000s. For newer buyers, this managerial move may serve as an entry point into a market that includes BBM, Takara, Calbee, and a unique run of home run-related issues tied directly to his career achievements.
The Shigeo Nagashima Connection Adds Historical Weight
Matsui’s return also resonates because of his close connection to Shigeo Nagashima, one of the most beloved figures in Japanese baseball history. Nagashima spent his entire playing career with the Giants from 1958 through 1974, batting .305 with 444 home runs. He later managed the club from 1975 to 1980 and again from 1993 to 2001, overlapping with Matsui’s Giants playing career.
Known widely as “Mr. Giants” and “Mr. Pro Yakyu,” Nagashima was far more than a former star. He was a symbol of the sport in Japan. After his death at age 89 on June 3, 2025, many fans found meaning in the timing and numerology surrounding the date, connecting it to his uniform number 3 and his place at third base. The emotional significance of his passing only deepened the importance of the players and stories most closely tied to him.
Matsui was one of those players. At Nagashima’s funeral, family remarks underscored just how much Matsui meant to the former Giants legend. Matsui also shared a story from their years together, recalling that he once asked about playing third base, only to be told that his place was in the outfield. Nagashima told him, “I want you to be Joe DiMaggio.”
That anecdote became even more meaningful later, when Matsui visited Nagashima’s home for swing work and saw a DiMaggio bat and a large image of the Yankees legend. Matsui came to understand exactly what Nagashima had in mind for him as a player. When the time came for Matsui to leave Japan for Major League Baseball, he referenced that conversation, telling his manager that if he was supposed to be Joe DiMaggio, then he was going to the Yankees.
Now that Matsui is returning to guide the Giants, collectors are not just looking at a former slugger taking a new job. They are looking at a major figure stepping into a role tied to one of the most important mentor-student relationships in Japanese baseball history.
Matsui’s Career Resume Still Drives Strong Hobby Interest
Matsui’s on-field record already gave him a strong collector base before the managerial news. Drafted by the Giants out of high school, he played for Yomiuri from 1993 through 2002 and hit 332 home runs for the club. He won three MVP awards in Japan and became one of the defining power hitters of his era there.
He then moved to MLB and added 175 more home runs while playing for the Yankees, Angels, A’s, and Rays. His most famous moment in the United States came with New York, where he earned 2009 World Series MVP honors. That blend of Japanese stardom and MLB success gives Matsui broader appeal than many players whose card markets are concentrated mainly in one country.
His total of 507 professional home runs between Japan and MLB also created the basis for one of the more unusual long-running card concepts attached to any modern player.
The NTV Home Run Cards Stand Out as a Signature Matsui Collectible
Among Matsui’s most distinctive issues is the Nippon Television home run card run celebrating each of his 507 career home runs. The series began in 1993 and continued throughout his career, creating a visual archive of his power production across different stages of his baseball life.
These cards are notable because they are built around specific home run moments. Rather than functioning as generic commemorative issues, the photographs show actual scenes connected to each blast, such as Matsui at the plate or circling the bases. For player collectors, that gives the run a documentary feel that is hard to replicate with standard base cards or later tribute releases.
The concept also gives Matsui collectors a built-in long-term chase. A single card is interesting. A complete run of 507 tells the story of his entire power career. That kind of project appeals to advanced player collectors who value completeness, chronology, and visual storytelling as much as rarity.
A collection of all of the NTV home run cards is displayed at the Matsui Hideki Baseball Museum in Ishikawa Prefecture, along with other memorabilia from his career. That museum presence further supports the importance of the set within the larger record of Matsui’s legacy.
Key Hideki Matsui Rookie Cards to Know
For many collectors, the first stop remains Matsui’s rookie-year cards from 1993. His best-known Japanese rookie is card #423 in the 1993 BBM set, a release that also includes Ichiro Suzuki’s rookie. That pairing has long made the set especially notable among modern Japanese issues.
While Ichiro’s card in the set frequently commands a significantly higher price, Matsui’s BBM rookie has remained relatively accessible compared with his stature in the sport. Reported market levels place raw or lower-grade examples around the $30 range, making it one of the more approachable key cards for a player of Matsui’s stature.
Collectors do need to watch for one important detail. A reprint of the 1993 BBM Matsui rookie was later included in the 2002 BBM “The Legend of Hideki Matsui” set. The reprint is marked “REPRINT” on the back, which provides a clear distinction, but it is still a point buyers should verify before purchasing an ungraded example.
Two other rookie-year cards from 1993 are also important for Matsui collectors:
- 1993 Takara Hideki Matsui
- 1993 Calbee Hideki Matsui
Recent reported sales cited for those cards included a PSA 8 Takara at $120 and a PSA 6 Calbee at $95. Those figures do not define the entire market, but they do show steady demand for Matsui’s Japanese rookie-year material, particularly when graded examples surface.
MLB Rookie-Year Appeal Still Matters
Matsui’s collecting profile is not limited to his Japan-issued cards. He also has a wide range of 2003 MLB rookie-year cards showing him in Yankees uniform, a category that continues to hold crossover appeal for both Japanese baseball collectors and mainstream MLB hobby buyers.
The Yankees connection remains especially important. Matsui was already a massive name when he arrived in the majors, and his New York years gave him a much larger international cardboard footprint through major U.S. manufacturers. Upper Deck and Topps both played a role in cards linked to his major league years, including home run-related issues and standard MLB releases.
That means the market for Matsui cards operates on two tracks at once. One track is rooted in Japanese issues, especially his 1993 rookie-year cards and the NTV home run series. The other is built around the visibility and collector familiarity of his Yankees-era cards. His return to the Giants may benefit both sides of that market, since renewed attention to his career often sends collectors searching across all phases of a player’s catalog.
Cards and Storylines Collectors May Watch Next
One of the more interesting hobby angles going forward is the possibility of new Japanese cards showing Matsui not as a player, but as the Giants’ manager. That distinction can matter more than it sounds. Collectors often respond strongly to first-year cards tied to a new role, particularly when the subject is a franchise legend returning to an iconic team.
Matsui will wear number 90 as Giants manager, the same number Nagashima wore when he began his own managerial run with the club. That detail strengthens the symbolic link between the two men and could become an especially meaningful note for collectors if future card issues highlight the continuity.
For player collectors, the most likely areas of increased attention include:
- 1993 BBM #423, especially original copies rather than the 2002 reprint
- 1993 Takara and 1993 Calbee rookies, particularly graded examples
- NTV home run cards, either singles tied to milestone blasts or longer runs
- 2003 Yankees rookie-year cards, which connect his Japanese stardom to his MLB arrival
- Future manager-era Japanese issues, if they are released with strong Giants branding or tribute themes
Collectors who favor legacy-driven markets often respond when a player’s story becomes easier to tell in full. Matsui now checks multiple boxes in that regard: Yomiuri icon, MLB success story, World Series MVP, student of Shigeo Nagashima, and now manager of Japan’s most prominent franchise.
What to Keep in Mind Before Buying
As attention rises, collectors should stay selective. Condition remains critical, especially for 1990s Japanese issues that can vary significantly in centering, edge wear, and surface quality. Authentication of reprints versus originals is also essential, particularly with the 1993 BBM rookie. Graded examples may offer more confidence, but raw cards can still be appealing if the seller provides clear front-and-back images.
It is also worth separating broad interest from immediate price spikes. Matsui’s market may gain momentum because of the managerial news, but the most durable value usually sits with cards that already matter historically: true rookie-year issues, scarce or iconic player-specific sets, and cards tied to signature career achievements.
For Matsui, that means his foundation remains strong. The 1993 BBM rookie anchors his Japanese card story. The Takara and Calbee issues provide alternate rookie-year paths. The 507-home run NTV run offers one of the most distinctive player collecting challenges in the sport. And his Yankees-era releases connect him to one of baseball’s largest global collecting audiences.
With Matsui back in a Giants uniform, this time in the dugout rather than the batter’s box, collectors have a fresh reason to revisit a career that already carried significance in two baseball worlds.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees’ Jazz Chisholm Oddly Similar to 270-Pound Catcher
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: When MLB teams consider whether to sign free agents to deals, they can't just consider what the player has done in the past. They have to consider what a player will do in the future. That's the task this offseason for anyone contemplating a contract for Jazz Chisholm Jr., and that includes the New York Yankees, who could choose to bring back Chisholm if the price is right. item.content:encoded:
When MLB teams consider whether to sign free agents to deals, they can't just consider what the player has done in the past. They have to consider what a player will do in the future.
That's the task this offseason for anyone contemplating a contract for Jazz Chisholm Jr., and that includes the New York Yankees, who could choose to bring back Chisholm if the price is right.
Baseball is a game with as much statistical history as any, and so it's often possible to try and draw conclusions about players who have come before.
In this case, does the long history of baseball provide clues about the type of player Chisholm will be going forward?
Maybe it can, but it also can bring up quite the oddities if you dig deeply enough.
Like, for example, that Chisholm is oddly similar to a 270-pound catcher.
Jazz Chisholm Similarity to Evan Gattis
Baseball Reference's vast database includes a cool tool known as the "Similarity Score." It looks at the scope of a player's career and identifies who that player has the most in common with statistically throughout baseball history.
The player that Chisholm is second-most similar to in all of baseball history is Evan Gattis.
Gattis, pictured above, was a hefty catcher with a big beard who ended up playing some left field and a lot of DH.
At his peak, Gattis sprayed powerful line drives all over the ballpark.
Of course, Chisholm and Gattis seem nothing alike, so how does this work?
The score isn't putting a ton of stock into the fact that Chisholm steals a lot of bases and Gattis doesn't. Instead, it's looking a lot at their high slugging percentage compared to a low batting average during different seasons along the way — sort of a look under the hood at how each guy has been productive at the plate.
In this case, it likely doesn't give a lot of clues how Chisholm will fare as a free agent. It's hard to predict how an athlete like him will age relative to a sturdy fella like Gattis.
It's ironic to think about, though — and for those wondering, Chisholm is listed as most similar to current Astros slugger Isaac Paredes. Maybe all this says that Chisholm is meant to play in Houston.
Yankees Future
Chisholm spoke positively about the Yankees at the end of the season. It seems likely that he'd return if New York would have him.
The Yankees, though, might have a positional logjam that they have to work through, and so it's a complicated equation in the Bronx.
There might be a team out there willing to give Chisholm a huge contract, and if that's the case, the Yanks might have to let him go. But maybe they'll find the money in their coffers to keep around an athletic second baseman with a bizarrely similar statistical profile to a bulky catcher.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Yankees' Jazz Chisholm Oddly Similar to 270-Pound Catcher appeared first on HEAVY.

item.content:encoded:
Cards
Former MLB, Japanese star Hideki Matsui a Giant again, giving his top cards historical significance
It had been the hope of Japanese baseball legend Shigeo Nagashima that Hideki Matsui would one day return to manage his beloved Yomiuri Giants.
Nagashima, who was known as “Mr. Giants,” “Mr. Pro Yakyu” (Pro Baseball) and simply “Mister,” played for the Yomiuri Giants his entire career, from 1958-74. He pleased the crowd by playing the game with much flair and teamed with slugger Sadaharu Oh to win championship after championship. After retiring with a .305 average and 444 home runs, Nagashima managed the Giants from 1975-1980 and then again, this time with Matsui on the team, from 1993-2001.
Related Content:
Nagashima is widely considered the most popular baseball player ever in Japan. When he died at the age of 89 on June 3, 2025, there were even some who found special meaning in the specific time and date that Nagashima died, which was on 6/3 at 6:39 in the morning. All of these numbers are divisible by 3, Shigeo’s uniform number as a player. Not only that, but Nagashima played third base. Fans also pointed out that the age Nagashima lived to, 89, must be symbolic, since one way to read the number 8 in Japanese is “ya,” and the number 9 is “kyu.” Put the 8 and 9 together, and you get the word for baseball, “yakyu.”
At Nagashima’s funeral, his daughter Mina said that her father “loved Matsui more than anything in the world,” and then added, “I have seriously thought that if Mr. Matsui and I were drowning in the sea at the same time, my father would save Mr. Matsui first.”
Mina remembered that when Matsui retired at the age of 38, her father remarked that he retired at 38, just like Matsui. “He appeared a little sad,” Mina said, describing the moment. “But there was also a look of pride on his face.”
Matsui traveled from his home in the States for the funeral in Japan, and in his speech he told a story about asking his manager if he could try playing third base. Nagashima, the former third baseman, told Matsui that without question his place was to be in the outfield. “I want you to be Joe DiMaggio,” Nagashima said.
At first, Matsui did not get the meaning of this statement. But on a later occasion, when Matsui went to Nagashima’s house to practice his swing, he saw a bat of DiMaggio and a large photo of Joltin’ Joe.
“I then understood that Mister really liked DiMaggio,” Matsui said. “I was happy that he told me that he wanted me to be that kind of player.”
When Matsui decided to head to the big leagues, he knew it would be a great disappointment for Nagashima. “Manager, you said Joe DiMaggio,” Matsui said when he went to see Nagashima. “So I am going to the Yankees.”
At this, Matsui received a big smile from Nagashima, and when Matsui saw that smile he finally thought, although it was difficult, that after all it would be okay to leave the Giants. But later Nagashima looked forward to the day that Matsui would come back.
The Giants introduced Matsui, 52, as their new manager on October 23. It might be called the most high-profile job in sports in Japan. The Giants are the most historically great and polarizing team in Nippon Professional Baseball. Giants fans are by no means limited to Tokyo but are everywhere in the country.
Matsui was drafted by the Giants out of high school and went on to slam 332 home runs over 10 years with the team, from 1993-2002. Matsui hit 175 more homers in his major league career with the Yankees, Angels, A’s, and Rays. He won three MVP awards in Japan and was the 2009 World Series MVP with the Yankees.
A Nippon Television (NTV) card set celebrating each of his 507 home runs was issued throughout his career, starting in 1993 (the major league home run cards were made by Upper Deck and then later Topps). The photos on these unique cards actually show a moment from each of his home runs, whether it is Matsui at the plate or rounding the bases. A collection of NTV cards of all of the home runs is displayed, along with other Matsui memorabilia, at the Matsui Hideki Baseball Museum, which is operated by Hideki’s family and located in Ishikawa prefecture.
Matsui’s main Japanese rookie card is #423 in the 1993 BBM set, which also contains Ichiro Suzuki’s rookie. While Ichiro’s rookie often sells for $200 dollars or more, Matsui’s can be had for around $30. Just be careful when buying one, as there is a reprint of the card that is part of a 2002 BBM “The Legend of Hideki Matsui” set. This card is clearly marked “REPRINT” on the back.
Two other 1993 rookie cards were made by Takara and Calbee, and there are many 2003 major league rookie cards of Matsui in Yankees threads. Recent sales of the 1993 cards include a Takara graded PSA 8 for $120 and a Calbee graded PSA 6 for $95.
Now Giants fans will get to see Hideki in a Giants uniform once again, and collectors will have a chance at Japanese cards of Matsui as a manager. He will wear number 90, the same number that Nagashima wore when he started out as manager of the Giants.
— SCD contributor Matt Bosch lived in Japan and went to his first professional baseball game in Japan 20 years ago and has been a fan ever since. He taught at a university in Japan and enjoys researching and writing about Japanese baseball."

item.title: [Empire Sports Media] Yankees need a real job for Jasson Dominguez or a trade
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: Keeping Jasson Dominguez is easy. Finding him a useful job on the Yankees is the part that needs an answer this winter. I wouldn’t trade him just to clear a locker. But another season planned around spare at-bats and somebody else’s injury would be a poor use of a player the organization still needs to evaluate. New York should either establish a credible route to regular work or find out what another club would offer. Mark Polishuk’s new offseason outlook for MLB Trade Rumors opens with the nee
item.content:encoded:
Keeping Jasson Dominguez is easy. Finding him a useful job on the Yankees is the part that needs an answer this winter.
I wouldn’t trade him just to clear a locker. But another season planned around spare at-bats and somebody else’s injury would be a poor use of a player the organization still needs to evaluate. New York should either establish a credible route to regular work or find out what another club would offer.
Mark Polishuk’s new offseason outlook for MLB Trade Rumors opens with the need to remake New York’s one-dimensional offense. How Dominguez fits is one decision I’d put inside that review. Exploring a trade is my recommendation, not a report that the Yankees have a deal lined up.
The Yankees shouldn’t rewrite his 2026 season
This isn’t an argument that Dominguez spent the entire year sitting. He appeared in 57 major-league games and had 222 plate appearances. His defensive record includes 42 starts in right field and two in left, plus work at DH. He received real opportunities during the season.
The results were disappointing: a .225 average, .267 on-base percentage and .368 slugging percentage. His .635 OPS fell well below the .719 he produced in 429 plate appearances in 2025. Ten walks against 48 strikeouts didn’t give him much protection when the hits weren’t coming.
Those numbers explain the diminished confidence. They don’t make 222 plate appearances a final judgment on his bat. Dominguez had a better on-base season a year earlier, and trading him after the weaker one could mean accepting a return that doesn’t reflect his remaining upside.
There is a defensive question, too. His 2026 major-league fielding record has no center-field entry. That doesn’t prove he can’t play there. It does mean the Yankees shouldn’t describe him as their ready-made center-field insurance without a fresh evaluation of that assignment.
Competition has to offer something he can win
A legitimate spring competition would be a reason to keep him. A bench label with no clear way to gain at-bats would be much harder to defend. The distinction matters when the Yankees decide which outfielders and bats to bring into camp.
I’d explore his trade market while leaving room for the possibility that the best offer is no offer at all. There is no verified package to assess yet, and moving him for an insignificant return wouldn’t solve a development failure. If New York keeps Dominguez, the next roster plan should identify where he can play, whose at-bats are available and what performance would earn him more of them.
More about:New York Yankees

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Ryan McMahon Clearly Doesn't Fit in the Yankees' 2027 Plans After Boone's Luis Garcia Statement
item.dc:creator: Jovan Alford; Unknown
item.description: When Yankees manager Aaron Boone met with reporters via Zoom last week, he answered questions regarding his future with the club, this season, and the roster heading into next season. Many Yankees fans are looking for change on the roster this offseason, especially at second and third base, given what they saw from Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Ryan McMahon. Boone made one suggestion to remedy both issues: Luis Garcia Jr., who played well at first base and added another quality left-handed bat to the li
item.content:encoded:
When Yankees manager Aaron Boone met with reporters via Zoom last week, he answered questions regarding his future with the club, this season, and the roster heading into next season.
Many Yankees fans are looking for change on the roster this offseason, especially at second and third base, given what they saw from Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Ryan McMahon. Boone made one suggestion to remedy both issues: Luis Garcia Jr., who played well at first base and added another quality left-handed bat to the lineup.
However, fans aren’t exactly enthused by Garcia seeing time at second base. He played at second and shortstop for most of his career with the Washington Nationals and struggled defensively (-18 Outs Above Average and -17 Defensive Runs Saved at second base). He hasn’t played at the hot corner in the majors, but did so in the minors (36 games) in 2018, which was eight years ago, so that comes with its own set of obstacles.
But the fact that the Yankees are open to putting Garcia at a position he hasn’t played since he was 18 years old is a damning statement for McMahon.
Ryan McMahon’s future in pinstripes is seemingly hanging by a thread
As we all know, McMahon’s 2026 season in the Bronx was one to forget. His play at the plate and on the field is why fans want to see the Yankees sign Teruaki Sato this winter (even if it's a pipe dream) or consider a trade for Isaac Paredes.
The 31-year-old McMahon slashed .213/.279/.357 with 11 home runs, 41 RBI, and a .635 OPS in 124 games with the Yankees. Simply put, it was a continuation of what fans saw last year from the infielder after being acquired from the Colorado Rockies at the trade deadline (.208/.308/.333 with four home runs, 18 RBI, and a .641 OPS).
However, McMahon’s defense at third base was still somewhat respectable. In 2025, he had a .971 fielding percentage, 7 Defensive Runs Saved Above Average, and four errors.
But this season was a completely different story for McMahon on defense. He recorded a .960 fielding percentage, which was higher than the league average (.958), but had nine errors and -3 Defensive Runs Saved Above Average.
We also saw McMahon’s defense, or lack thereof, in the ALDS against the Tampa Bay Rays, where he threw an ugly first-inning error in Game 2, which led to an early run. The Yankees went on to lose, 5-2, at Tropicana Field.
If it were up to Yankees fans, they would trade McMahon this offseason and drive him to the airport. But based on his production this season, it’s hard to believe he will have a bunch of suitors, even though he will be a free agent after the 2027 season.
McMahon is set to make $16 million, which isn’t a small price for a team to pay. The Yankees will likely have to eat some cash or take a bad contract in a trade for McMahon, which doesn’t sound appealing either.
There’s also the DFA route with McMahon. But if you’re general manager Brian Cashman, the goal is to get value in return, even if it’s a lower-level prospect. Then you figure out third base, whether that’s Garcia, Anthony Volpe, or another player who could be available this winter.
Jovan has over 13 years of experience in sports media, including stops at The Philadelphia Tribune, SB Nation, FanSided and Hoops Habit. Most recently joining OnSI, his teams covered include the New York Jets, New York Yankees and New York Knicks.

item.content:encoded:
The Atlanta Braves are currently at home for the offseason.
Despite a strong 2026 regular season, they were eliminated by the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 4 of the NLDS.
The final game was lost by a score of 4-1 at Truist Park on October 7.
Ex-Braves Star Owed Over $170 Million
Now that their season is over, it’s worth taking a look at a former Braves star.
Max Fried is coming off his second year pitching for the New York Yankees.
He went 5-5 with a 2.80 ERA in 20 starts.
Max Fried #54 of the New York Yankees looks on during the first inning in game three of the American League Division Series against the Tampa Bay Rays at Yankee Stadium on October 07, 2026 in the Bronx borough of New York City.
It’s also worth noting that the Yankees owe Fried (who is 32) $174 million over the next six seasons.
He will make $29 million per year until becoming a free agent after the 2032 season (h/t Spotrac).
Bob Nightengale of USA Today wrote (on December 10, 2024): “The Max Fried eight-year, $218 million contract is the largest for a left-handed pitcher, and fourth by any pitcher in history. No deferrals. No opt-outs.”
Looking At Fried’s Time In Atlanta
Max Fried #54 of the Atlanta Braves speaks to the media during Gatorade All-Star Workout Day at Globe Life Field on July 15, 2024 in Arlington, Texas.
Fried was picked in the 1st round of the 2012 MLB Draft by the San Diego Padres.
He spent the first eight seasons of his MLB career with the Braves.
During that time period, Fried made two trips to the All-Star Game (and was part of the team that won the 2021 World Series title over the Houston Astros).
Looking At Fried’s Time In The Bronx
Max Fried #54 of the New York Yankees throws a live bullpen session before a game against the Detroit Tigers at Yankee Stadium on June 30, 2026 in New York City.
Fried made the 2025 All-Star Game in his first year with the Yankees.
He went 19-5 with a 2.86 ERA in 32 starts.
That said, Fried had a 6.75 ERA in two postseason starts in 2025 (and was the losing pitcher in Game 3 of the 2026 ALDS against the Tampa Bay Rays).

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are coming off another strong regular season.
That said, they also had another letdown in the postseason.
After sweeping the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, the Yankees got swept by the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
They lost the final game (at home in the Bronx) by a score of 4-3.
New York Yankees Will Pay 34-Year-Old $27 Million
With the season over, it’s worth taking a look at Carlos Rodon.
The 33-year-old (who will turn 34 in December) is coming off a strong regular season.
He went 7-3 with a 2.67 ERA in 16 starts.
Chris Kirschner of The Athletic wrote (on September 16): “Carlos Rodón, who regained some velocity as his outing progressed, has not allowed more than three runs in 25 straight starts. It is the longest streak in Yankees history and tied for the sixth-longest streak in MLB history.”
Carlos Rodon #55 of the New York Yankees delivers a pitch in the first inning against the New York Mets at Yankee Stadium on September 11, 2026 in The Bronx borough of New York City. The New York Yankees and the New York Mets are wearing hats to honor first responders on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attack on New York during the game.
It’s also worth mentioning that the Yankees still owe Rodon a lot of money.
He will be paid $27 million during the 2027 season (h/t Spotrac).
ESPN’s Jeff Passan wrote (on December 15, 2022): “Left-hander Carlos Rodón and the New York Yankees are in agreement on a six-year, $162 million contract, sources familiar with the deal tell ESPN.”
Rodon will become a free agent following the 2028 MLB season.
Looking At Rodon
Carlos Rodon #55 of the New York Yankees pitches in the fourth inning against the Baltimore Orioles at Oriole Park at Camden Yards on August 18, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland.
Rodon was picked in the 1st round of the 2014 MLB Draft.
He spent the first seven years of his career playing for the Chicago White Sox.
After Chicago, Rodon (who is a three-time MLB All-Star) had a quick stint with the San Francisco Giants.
Samantha Busch, Ashley Rodón and Carlos Rodón attend the Carlos Rodón Foundation 2026 Willow Gala at the Refinery on August 24, 2026 in Brooklyn, New York.
Rodon has 100 career wins with a 3.67 ERA.

Blake's extension comes on the heels of the Yankees retaining manager Aaron Boone and general manager Bria
item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

25 Oct 2026, 00:49 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Kim Klement Neitzel)
It was not a banner year for the New York Yankees, but the organization appears prepared to stay with the same coaching group for 2027. In their latest move, the Yankees have agreed to sign pitching coach Matt Blake to a three-year contract extension, according to the New York Post.
Blake's extension comes on the heels of the Yankees retaining manager Aaron Boone and general manager Brian Cashman. New York had the American League's highest payroll ($310 million) last season, but did not make it past the AL Division Series for the second year in a row.
The Yankees' 2026 season ended in disappointment, as New York (93-68) finished 4-1/2 games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East and then were swept in the playoffs by the Rays.
Blake, for his part, seemed to hold up his end of the bargain, overseeing a staff that included Cy Young contender Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA) and an effective return from Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61). Will Warren gave the group a third 10-game winner (11-6, 3.92), but Max Fried (5-5, 2.80) and Carlos Rodon (7-3, 2.67) missed large chunks of the season due to injury.
The Yankees finished first in the majors with a 3.23 team ERA under the 41-year-old Blake, who has been the team's pitching coach since the 2020 season.
--Field Level Media

In a message posted by the Yankees, the club wished Matsui well in his new chapter with the team where he spent all 10 seasons of his Japanese playing career. A Yankees favorite returns to his first baseball home Yankees fans know the October version of Matsui best. He won the 20
item.content:encoded:
Hideki Matsui is going back to Yomiuri with a different job. The former Yankees star has been introduced as the Japanese club’s new manager, MLB’s Max Ralph reported Friday.
New York quickly offered its congratulations. In a message posted by the Yankees, the club wished Matsui well in his new chapter with the team where he spent all 10 seasons of his Japanese playing career.
A Yankees favorite returns to his first baseball home
Yankees fans know the October version of Matsui best. He won the 2009 World Series MVP award after going 8-for-13 with three home runs and eight RBIs against Philadelphia. That was the finish to seven seasons in New York, from 2003 through 2009.
But Yomiuri isn’t a sentimental stop on the way to some other job. Matsui was already a major star there before joining the Yankees. His move into the dugout brings him back to the organization where he won three Central League MVP awards and three Japan Series titles as a player.
That history helps explain the attention around this appointment. He isn’t arriving as a familiar name with no connection to the club. He knows what wearing that uniform meant long before his years in the Bronx.
The playing record is secure; managing is a new assignment
Matsui finished his major-league career with 175 home runs and an .822 OPS over 10 seasons. Those numbers establish what he did with a bat. They don’t tell us how he’ll handle a struggling player, balance a lineup or make a late-game decision from the bench.
That’s what makes the move more interesting than another ceremonial appearance. He’ll have responsibility for other players’ opportunities and for decisions that don’t come with the immediate feedback of his own at-bats.
For clarity, this is a Yomiuri appointment, not a Yankees coaching move or evidence of a change to New York’s staff. The Yankees are celebrating a former champion taking on a new job. Matsui now gets the much less ceremonial work of managing the club that first made him a star.
More about:New York Yankees

item.title: [yanksgoyard.com] 3 offseason mistakes Yankees seem uniquely poised to make this winter
item.dc:creator: Colin Keane
item.description: The New York Yankees finished 2026 with one of the better pitching staffs in baseball and a good amount of talent in their lineup ... all to bow out in the ALDS for a second straight season. Yankees fans are beyond frustrated, former Yankees are frustrated, and yet nothing's apparently going to change from a leadership perspective. Aaron Boone's coming back in 2027, and Brian Cashman announced on Wednesday that he will receive a new contract, too. Since Cashman's return has always seemed so obvi
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees finished 2026 with one of the better pitching staffs in baseball and a good amount of talent in their lineup ... all to bow out in the ALDS for a second straight season. Yankees fans are beyond frustrated, former Yankees are frustrated, and yet nothing's apparently going to change from a leadership perspective. Aaron Boone's coming back in 2027, and Brian Cashman announced on Wednesday that he will receive a new contract, too.
Since Cashman's return has always seemed so obvious and preconceived, I'm not even going to include that in the following rundown of three mistakes the Yankees will hurt themselves with this winter. But if you wanted to include the fact that they didn't part with Boone and are going to re-up Cashman (for how long, who knows), this list could easily be five. Let's get into it.
3 mistakes the Yankees will surely make this winter
1. They won’t trade from their young pitching surplus
The Yankees have too many good starters for a five- or even six-man rotation; meanwhile, they have holes everywhere else (Third baseman? Another outfielder? Bullpen?). Any competent GM would view this as a clear opportunity to trade a Will Warren or a Ryan Weathers for multiple depth pieces. Even Elmer Rodriguez might fetch legitimate value in this market.
Somehow, someway, Cashman will fail to cash in on any of his young, controllable arms, entering the season with an unhappy starter or two and a position player depth chart that doesn't look markedly improved. Yay!
2. They will keep believing in Giancarlo Stanton and fail to trade Ryan McMahon
Stanton and McMahon are "move on from this guy immediately" candidates for entirely different reasons. Stanton literally doesn't play baseball anymore, and McMahon can't field his position at an elite level anymore, which was the only thing he was offering the Yankees in the first place.
Would the Yankees need to eat some cash to move on from these declining pieces? Surely, and it's not like New York's been completely against doing this in the past. But the more likely outcome is that Cashman and the Yanks will rationalize the retention of both Stanton (he'll be load-managed!) and McMahon (he's still under contract!), since it would take legitimately clever front office work to move either without suffering financially.
3. They will underbuild the 2027 bullpen because 2026 went "well"
Speaking of rationalizing things that make no sense, Cashman has a habit of pointing to lucky or singular narratives from the past season and formulating a thesis that those narratives will continue into the next season. He did this when Trent Grisham's qualifying offer came up last winter: Cashman basically said that since Grisham had a career year (which he'd never come close to before, mind you), the Yankees believed Grisham would offer similar production in 2026. That didn't happen, of course.
This year's version of the "Grisham explanation" will apply to the bullpen. Cashman will look back on the success of New York's 'pen in 2026 (even though there were plenty of rocky stretches, and Paul Blackburn probably won't be back) and use this success as a reason not to over-exert himself on the market when it comes to beefing up the staff with relievers.
Look how good Brent Headrick was! He can pitch every night! We're not worried about the bullpen! Meanwhile, Cashman is bound to run Headrick into the ground midway through 2027. And David Bednar, for that matter. The Yankees of recent years derive some weird enjoyment out of entering new seasons with an undermanned bullpen, and then watching the deadline go by without doing much about it. It's hard to expect that to change this winter.

item.content:encoded:
Derek Jeter, David Ortiz And Alex Rodriguez Make Their World Series Predictions
After finishing the MLB regular season with the best records in their respective conferences, the Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers now must go through each other for their first-ever World Series trophy, and the FOX Sports MLB desk is expecting a fight to the finish line.
Here is who World Series-winners Derek Jeter, David Ortiz and Alex Rodriguez are predicting will take home the Commissioner's Trophy this year:
Big Papi, Derek Jeter and Alex Rodriguez unveil their 2026 World Series predictions
Jeter: It’s a tough one because these teams mirror each other. They both do great things, but I think I’m going with the home field advantage and the bullpen of the Milwaukee Brewers. Brewers in 7.
Ortiz: I’ve got to tell you: the American League is a hard league to play. This team led the league from the very beginning to the end, winning all of the time. So, I’ve got to go Tampa Bay in 7.
Rodriguez: Best two teams, best two defenses, the best two everything. I'm going with home field advantage on a walk-off, the Brewers in 7.

item.content:encoded:
The World Series is set to start Friday night, and the New York Yankees for the 16th time in the last 17 years are not in it.
It was 16 days ago that the Yankees were ousted from the postseason, swept in three games by the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Division Series. In the final game, that sealed the Yankees’ fate for another season, starting pitcher Max Fried was one of the reasons the Bronx Bombers lost and went home.
Fried lasted 5 2/3 innings and gave up four runs on seven hits including two home runs, but those four runs were one too many as the Yankees fell to the Rays 4-3.
As they look toward 2027, the Yankees still owe Max Fried $174 million. That’s the total remaining on his contract which extends through the 2032 season, according to Spotrac‘s contract breakdown. None of Fried’s Yankees salary is deferred.
After an injury-marred season, Fried’s payroll tab jumps from $14.5 million to $31.5 million in 2027, according to Spotrac.
Fried signed the eight-year, $218 million contract in December 2024, a record for a left-hander that topped David Price’s seven-year deal with the Boston Red Sox by $1 million, according to The Associated Press.
Half of the $20 million signing bonus arrived on Jan. 31, 2025, and the other half on Jan. 31, 2026, according to The Associated Press reporting.
Spotrac lists the full $218 million as guaranteed. “No deferrals. No opt-outs,” wrote USA Today‘s Bob Nightengale.
New York Yankees’ Max Fried Contract Money Owed by Year
Fried collected $22 million in cash payments in each of 2025 and 2026 (a $12 million salary plus a $10 million bonus installment), which puts the Yankees’ actual outlay at $44 million so far, according to Spotrac.
The remaining $174 million comes due at $29 million a year from 2027 through 2032. The balance falls to $145 million after 2027, $116 million after 2028, $87 million after 2029, $58 million after 2030 and $29 million after 2031.
For luxury tax purposes, the deal counts at $27.25 million a year. The payroll charge rises to $31.5 million in 2027 because the $29 million salary replaces the $12 million one, while the bonus stays prorated at $2.5 million annually. Spotrac also lists a full no-trade clause.
Fried’s 2026 Season, Playoffs and Career
Fried went 5-5 with a 2.80 ERA and a 0.99 WHIP in 20 starts, striking out 104 and walking 33 over 112 2/3 innings in 2026.
Two trips to the injured list for a bone bruise in his pitching elbow cut the workload. Manager Aaron Boone said Wednesday that new imaging showed the ligament in Fried’s left elbow in good shape, and he was not expected to have any arm issues in his offseason training program.
In 2025, his first season in pinstripes, Fried went 19-5 with a 2.86 ERA and a 1.10 WHIP in 32 starts, striking out 189 over 195 1/3 innings, according to Spotrac. His ERA fell by 0.06 in 2026 and his WHIP by 0.11, while his innings dropped by about 83.
In the postseason, Fried beat the Boston Red Sox in Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series on Sept. 30, allowing one run over six innings. A week later, he took the loss in ALDS Game 3 against the Tampa Bay Rays. He finished the postseason 1-1 with a 3.86 ERA and 13 strikeouts in 11 2/3 innings.
Fried, a Santa Monica, California, native, pitched at Harvard-Westlake School in Los Angeles alongside Jack Flaherty and Lucas Giolito, according to The Associated Press. The San Diego Padres drafted him seventh overall in 2012, and Atlanta acquired him in the 2014 trade that sent Justin Upton to San Diego, according to Spotrac.
He reached the majors with the Braves in 2017 and won the clincher of the 2021 World Series. Adding his 2026 line puts his career record at 97-46 with 1,156 strikeouts.
Fried turns 33 on Jan. 18, with six seasons and $174 million still ahead of him.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] One Offseason Mistake the Yankees Cannot Afford to Repeat

item.content:encoded:
With the World Series having kicked off in Milwaukee, the clock is ticking on the start of the MLB offseason. The minute it ends, all 30 teams are able to go to work on building towards 2027.
In those first few days, the Yankees will have exclusive negotiating rights with their free agents for five days and will be able to make decisions on whether they want to bring them back or not.
With no club or player options to sort out, the only mandatory decisions that the team has to make by the time the five-day period ends in early November are whether to tender the qualifying offer to David Bednar and Jazz Chisholm Jr.
Bednar seems likely to get one after his strong body of work in the Bronx, and his market value is likely stretching toward the $23 million that the qualifying offer is worth, but what about Chisholm? He was more than worth that number to start his Yankees career, and even in a down 2026, posted 3.5 fWAR off almost exclusively defense and baserunning value.
Despite his upside and floor, the Yankees should learn from their past and just cut ties with their second baseman instead of making a guaranteed money commitment that could hinder the rest of their offseason.
Why Trent Grisham's qualifying offer failure might doom Jazz Chisholm's bid for one
Last season around this time, the Yankees faced a similar decision with a player on the opposite end of the spectrum, Trent Grisham, someone who broke out in a big way in 2025 after years of being a typical fourth outfielder and suddenly was hitting the market off an All-Star-caliber season.
The Yankees extended Grisham a $22 million qualifying offer, which he accepted to the moderate surprise of the baseball world. Many believed that he would opt for long-term security off a contract year, but he accepted an opportunity to maximize his money now and set up a bigger payday in 2027 if he had another strong season.
That, of course, didn't happen. Grisham battled multiple hamstring ailments and slumped both with the glove and with his bat, not coming close to replicating what made him worth the qualifying offer in the first place.
The process of extending the offer to Grisham was not a bad process from management, who oversaw the development of a high-contact 29-year-old bat who seemingly fit like a glove atop the batting order, but injuries can always throw a curveball.
The bigger worry with Grisham wasn't the collapse risk, but rather how it tied up a lot of the Yankees' money early in the offseason. Management believed the 2025 team was worth running back, so the team spent a vast majority of their offseason budget retaining Grisham and Cody Bellinger at higher rates.
Fast forward to this offseason, where giving Chisholm a one-year prove-it deal doesn't seem like the worst in the world, but when you think about the team's limited budget to make the clear additions they need to make after Hal Steinbrenner aired out the offense's struggles, it doesn't seem like the smart move.
Despite his upside, it's best for Yankees to part ways with Chisholm
The other side of a qualifying offer is draft compensation, but as a luxury tax team, it's only a fourth-round pick. It's hardly a hedge to make.
Chisholm has all the ability in the world to get back to the dynamic 30/30 talent he was in 2025 as one of the best all-around second basemen in the sport. Hell, you can make the argument that Chisholm was one of the American League's best at the position even with his struggles. Just look at how awful Ernie Clement was after leading the Junior Circuit in All-Star voting!
It would certainly sting if the Yankees let Chisholm go elsewhere and he put his 2026 in the past, but the team can't afford to have him on the books for $23 million next year and have him not rebound. The onus has been put on the front office by ownership to overhaul the offense, and that's not possible if the team ties up most of their offseason budget in Chisholm and Bednar.
Michael is a contributing writer for Yankees On SI and is a student at Penn State University. In addition to On SI, he writes for PSU's student-run blog, Onward State, specializing in wrestling and baseball, as well as SB Nation's Posting & Toasting and Pinstripe Alley, covering the Knicks and Yankees.
Follow MichaelZeno24

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees Mailbag: A qualifying offer conundrum
item.dc:creator: Madison Pavich
item.description: Good afternoon everyone, it's time to dive back into the mailbag and answer some of your questions. The QO to Jazz also seems likely as Yankees will perceive he will reject it and, unlike the gamble with Grisham that was a huge miscalculation on Cashman's part, Jazz will probably reject it. Your thoughts? I don't kno
item.content:encoded:
Good afternoon everyone, it's time to dive back into the mailbag and answer some of your questions. Remember to send in your questions for our bi-weekly call by e-mail to pinstripealleyblog [at] gmail [dot] com.
Craig Z. asks: It would seem a qualifying offer to Bednar is a given. The QO to Jazz also seems likely as Yankees will perceive he will reject it and, unlike the gamble with Grisham that was a huge miscalculation on Cashman's part, Jazz will probably reject it. Your thoughts?
I don't know if I'd agree with your second point, as reports have come out saying that the team is actually unlikely to offer the qualifying offer to Jazz Chisholm Jr. this offseason. The gamble over whether Chisholm would accept the deal or not mirroring what happened with Trent Grisham last year is probably informing their decision on that matter, as while I wouldn't hate bringing Jazz back on a one-year deal the team seems to be angling towards allowing him to walk. Whereas Grisham was coming off of a career-best year, Chisholm had his worst season in pinstripes, but the argument could be made that Grisham knew the market was a lot more crowded with excellent choices while Chisholm is still one of the best options in a free agent field lacking a true superstar or even many stars to compete against.
With that in mind, it might be a more reasonable gamble to give Chisholm the QO and not lose him for nothing than it was with Grisham, but again the team clearly cares about their budget and potentially handing out over $45 million in 2027 salary between Bednar and Chisholm before free agency even opens might restrict them too much to make other moves. I'm not thrilled with the backup option to Chisholm being running Anthony Volpe at the keystone, but if it leads to improvements elsewhere on the roster I could see the logic in the move — and we'll talk about where that upgrade is most needed in a moment. Ultimately, while I know Chisholm had a disappointing year for New York (and perhaps set himself up to with talk of having a 50-50 season during spring), I think it's unlikely they field a better player at his position than him in 2027 and I think that makes the QO a worthwhile choice, but it looks like that won't be the case.
Anton H. asks: With Ryan McMahon struggling to solve the Yankees' third base problem as hoped, do you think the team will try to trade him this offseason, or is a DFA more likely? Given his $16 million salary for 2027, what teams, if any, could make a compelling case for acquiring him despite the financial commitment?
Now, here is where the resources need to be allocated to improve the position. Third base has been a black hole for damn near a decade at this point, with only small bursts of quality play like Gio Urshela's 2019 run sparkling before being swallowed back up by the void. Ryan McMahon was never expected to be a quality hitter when the Yankees acquired him, but they were certainly expecting better than the 78 wRC+ he posted in 124 games. He was also expected to overcome his offensive capabilities by providing stellar defense, and while he lived up to that in 2025 his play at the hot corner sizzled out completely in 2026 leading to a frustrating experience where he really didn't provide much of anything.
That's not really a compelling case to bring towards any potential suitors, so while the team would surely love to trade him away for whatever they could get, it would require tacking on prospects to get even partial salary relief at the moment. Normally I'd say they're better off just going the DFA route like they did with DJ LeMahieu and Aaron Hicks, but the team is also staring down the prospect of moving on from Giancarlo Stanton's contract as well and I'm not sure that Hal Steinbrenner could stomach two deadweight contracts for players not even on the team anymore. Of the two, it would be easier to sell McMahon with a prospect attached than it would Stanton, who has a full no-trade clause and an extra year on his deal even if it is a team option. If push comes to shove the team is better off moving on from McMahon and DFA'ing him would suffice, but if they can find an angle to move him that doesn't cost any of their blue chip prospects it wouldn't be a bad move to make — they can't all make it to the big leagues, and using prospect capital to improve the roster by subtraction is still an improvement. I trust the player development team to find enough talent to keep the pipeline greased up, and they didn't offload too much in this year's deadline.
jws85 asks: Assuming no additions during free agency, who would be the best leadoff hitter? Rice and Judge needs to be 2-4. Lombard, Bellinger, or Volpe could be options. Wells, García, Stanton, and Jones makes no sense.
If you're forcing me to keep Ben Rice and Aaron Judge somewhere in the 2-4 range then I'd set my sights on George Lombard Jr. earning the leadoff role, as the rookie showed solid results at the plate during his whirlwind debut in the second half and throughout the postseason. The defensive misplays were atypical of his performance down in the minors, but the bat showed some promise and the only other candidate I see would be Volpe, who has already had his chance to be a leadoff hitter to no avail. However, what I would rather do in this scenario is just have Rice hit leadoff, bat Judge second and have Bellinger flanking him with Lombard or Jones at cleanup and García hitting fifth. Rice proved that he's a capable enough table-setter, and without an ideal OBP-driven player in the lineup as is you might as well give your best hitters the earliest chances to get up to bat.

item.content:encoded:
ゴジラの帰還が、巨人に〝世界規模の夢〟をもたらす。巨人は２３日、松井秀喜新監督（５２）の就任を正式発表。都内のホテルで山口寿一オーナーと会見した新指揮官は、２４年ぶりに古巣へ復帰し、背番号「９０」のユニホームに袖を通した。注目は采配だけではない。ＭＬＢで築いた規格外の人脈が、名だたるメジャーリーガーの大型補強や超豪華な指導陣を呼び寄せる可能性が出始めている。
日米通算５０７本塁打の大スターが古巣の命運を背負う。「今日は満面の笑顔で自分の故郷に戻ってきたつもりです」。松井監督は就任会見で、そう語り「これからのジャイアンツに新たな黄金時代が訪れるよう、今日ここからスタートしていきたい」と宣言した。
山口オーナーも「強いジャイアンツにしていくには、松井監督にお願いするしかない」と期待を込めた。契約は３年。恩師・長嶋茂雄氏が監督時代に着けた「９０」を背負い、３０日から始まる秋季キャンプで本格始動する。「指導者の経験はほぼありません」と自ら認めたが、手持ちのカードが乏しいわけではない。
新体制の最大の武器となり得るのが、現役、引退後の２０年以上で培った〝ＭＬＢ人脈〟だ。松井監督はヤンキースのＧＭ特別アドバイザーとして１２年間、傘下の若手育成に尽力。現主将兼主砲のアーロン・ジャッジ外野手もマイナー時代の教え子。２０１５年には打撃の体の使い方を直接伝授した。
ならば将来的にジャッジが選手として、師匠が新指揮官となった巨人のユニホームに袖を通したら――。実現すれば、球界騒然の超大型補強だ。一方、ヤンキース時代に親交を深めた元主将デレク・ジーター氏や、０９年の世界一をともに味わったアレックス・ロドリゲス氏ら大物ＯＢには、臨時コーチ就任や将来の入閣という夢も膨らむ。
松井監督は会見で「選手が自分自身で成長できるように」と力説した。米球界の練習法やデータ活用を巨人流に取り込み、若手が自ら課題を克服できる環境を整えてこそ、その人脈は真価を発揮する。
人脈はグラウンドの外にも広がる。ヤンキースのブライアン・キャッシュマンＧＭに加え、エンゼルス在籍時のアート・モレノ・オーナー、アスレチックス在籍時の編成トップで現上級顧問のビリー・ビーン氏。エンゼルスは球団売却で合意済みだが、人脈の幅広さは際立つ。１２年の現役最後に在籍したレイズの編成トップは、現ドジャース編成本部長のアンドリュー・フリードマン氏。こうした球団との縁が助っ人の獲得や育成、情報交換に生きない手はない。
数字では測れない選手の適応力や人柄を見極めるには、現地の情報が欠かせないはずだ。交渉はフロントの仕事でも、松井監督の助言が〝掘り出し物〟の獲得につながるかもしれない。
ＭＬＢの現行労使協定は１２月１日（日本時間２日）に失効予定。ロックアウトとなった場合、ＭＬＢは選手がその間、ＮＰＢなどでプレーすることを認める方針を各球団に通達したと報じられている。来春まで長期化すれば、超大物の一時的な来日も想定される。一方でジャッジにはヤンキースとの長期契約があり、本人の意向や球団間の調整も含めハードルは高い。それでも師弟の縁を生かしたロックアウト中の短期加入、あるいは松井監督の在任中に実現する数年先の大型補強という構想は十分に描ける。
松井監督は「今、世界一の野球選手が日本人であることも事実です」と述べ、巨人から世界に通用する選手を育てる決意を示した。巨人の理念は「アメリカ野球に追いつけ、追い越せ」――。その理想を、海の向こうで得た〝スーパーコネクション〟を武器に実現できるか。新生巨人の夢は松井新監督を発信源に東京ドームの外、世界へ広がっている。

item.title: [ｄメニューニュース] MLB 「ご就任おめでとう」巨人・松井秀喜新監督、古巣ヤンキース祝福 粋な日本語エール 通算140発＆ワールドシリーズMVP受賞（SANSPO）｜ｄメニューニュース

item.content:encoded:
米大リーグ、ヤンキースが23日（日本時間24日）、プロ野球巨人の新監督に就任した松井秀喜氏（52）を祝福した。球団公式Xで「ヤンキースのレジェンドである松井秀喜さん、巨人の監督就任おめでとうございます。新たな門出のご活躍をお祈りしています」と英文で記載し、さらに「巨人軍の松井秀喜監督、ご就任おめでとうございます」と日本語で記した。
松井氏は2003年に巨人からヤンキースに移籍し、09年まで7年間プレー。04年には当時、日本選手のシーズン最多本塁打となる31本を放つなど、140本塁打をマーク。2009年には日本選手初のワールドシリーズMVPを受賞し、ニューヨーカーに愛される存在となった。
松井新監督は23日の就任会見で「きょう、ここに来る時、24年前、自らの意思でジャイアンツを去る日のことを思い出していました。あの日は笑顔を見せることができなかったですが、きょう満面の笑顔でふるさとに戻ってきたつもりです」と語っていた。

item.title: [roundtable.io] Aaron Judge's Disconnect With Yankees Grows Amid Latest Report
item.dc:creator: Matthew Schmidt
item.description: Apparently, Aaron Judge isn't in agreement with a whole lot the New York Yankees do. Judge has been at odds with Yankees management quite a bit recently, and things came to a head at the end of the 2026 campaign when the three-time AL MVP openly questioned the front office's dedication. A frustrated Judge told reporters that New York needed to be "all in" this offseason and that the Yankees need to actually get the right players. Those comments didn't sit well with Yankees brass, and owner Hal S
item.content:encoded:
Apparently, Aaron Judge isn't in agreement with a whole lot the New York Yankees do.
Judge has been at odds with Yankees management quite a bit recently, and things came to a head at the end of the 2026 campaign when the three-time AL MVP openly questioned the front office's dedication.
A frustrated Judge told reporters that New York needed to be "all in" this offseason and that the Yankees need to actually get the right players.
Those comments didn't sit well with Yankees brass, and owner Hal Steinbrenner took a slight jab at Judge during his recent press conference by saying that he felt New York was absolutely "all in" this past season given the money the team spent.
But Judge's issues with the Yanks didn't stop there.
He disagreed with Aaron Boone's public assessment of his calf injury, questioning why Boone would call it a "moderate" strain. He disagreed with how New York went about his recovery, leaving him off the Wild Card and Division Series rosters.
And apparently, Judge has also pushed back against the Yankees' development methods.
Chris Kirschner of The Athletic has reported that Judge was one of four players — with Jazz Chisholm, Trent Grisham and Ryan McMahon being the other three — who had little to no interest in attempting to improve using analytics.
Those aren't exactly the players to whom you wanted to be tied if you're Judge.
Chisholm and Grisham will both be departing via free agency after dreadful seasons. McMahon has long been an essential dead spot in the Yankee lineup.
And considering that Steinbrenner made it clear that he was not happy with New York's offensive performance this season, you can bet he is none too pleased that Judge basically refused assistance.
Not that Judge needs it. He is one of the best hitters of his generation, and I do think analytics are a bit overstated. Yes, they're important, but there is no doubt that some people get a bit carried away with them as a be-all-end-all strategy.
However, because Judge is the captain, he is expected to set an example, and shirking the opportunity to improve is certainly not a good look.
Clearly, Judge is at odds with a whole lot of what the Yankees are doing right now, but given the fact that he missed the majority of 2026 — and all of the playoffs — due to multiple injuries and hasn't exactly been a prime time performer in October, he doesn't really have much of a leg to stand on at the moment.
Judge is 34 years old. He took less money to re-sign with the Yankees before 2023. His frustration is understandable. But he is also culpable for New York having not won a World Series throughout his tenure with the club.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] The Yankees' Hal Steinbrenner-Aaron Judge 'feud' is just a fan invention
item.dc:creator: Anthony Ranaudo
item.description: When I saw a tweet saying Hal Steinbrenner "shot a flamethrower" at Yankees captain Aaron Judge, I had my popcorn ready for the fireworks. I watched it once, then again, waiting for a shot that never came. After the Rays swept the Yankees out of the ALDS, Judge said he was "hating every single moment" of the elimination and that the front office should go all-in and "do what they need to do" to fill the roster's holes. People heard a captain calling out his owner, but I heard a guy whose season
item.content:encoded:
When I saw a tweet saying Hal Steinbrenner "shot a flamethrower" at Yankees captain Aaron Judge, I had my popcorn ready for the fireworks. I watched it once, then again, waiting for a shot that never came.
After the Rays swept the Yankees out of the ALDS, Judge said he was "hating every single moment" of the elimination and that the front office should go all-in and "do what they need to do" to fill the roster's holes. People heard a captain calling out his owner, but I heard a guy whose season had just ended, and not at all how he drew it up.
Why Hal Steinbrenner's Aaron Judge comments are a good sign for the Yankees
You have to remember what Judge's year looked like. A broken rib cost him more than three months, and a week after he returned, a calf strain put him right back on the injured list. When you're making $40 million a year and can't be on the field when your team needs you, it eats at you, and can take an emotional toll. His coaches and teammates know he wants to be out there, but it doesn't change the facts. I've sat in the clubhouse after a season ends, and I can promise you the first thought is not what they need to say to the media, and I think that's what a lot of people "felt" from Judge's comments.
Then, on Wednesday, Hal confirmed that a new deal for Brian Cashman is being worked out, and addressed Judge directly. He said he wasn't upset about the comments after the elimination game, that he had a "great conversation" with Judge the day before, and that with decisions coming after the World Series, Judge "is going to be a part of all that."
That's not a flamethrower. That's an owner who knows he has one of the greatest hitters ever for a limited window, and bringing the captain into roster conversations is how you protect a culture and redesign a winning one. Aaron Judge has earned every bit of that access.
He also said he has expectations of his players, mentioning the medical staff in the process, and (I think) some fans took that as the jab. I took it as the opposite. Judge set a standard after Game 3, and Hal agreed with him. An owner and a captain holding everyone to the same bar is exactly where you want this franchise, especially with so much uncertainty heading into this offseason's CBA.
Hal continued on and made sure to mention (maybe this is the jab?) that this team had the highest payroll in franchise history, and hasn't been shy about spending. Spending the most money and spending it on the right players aren't always the same thing, as plenty of expensive Yankees rosters have learned. Still, if I'm Judge, I'll take an owner who's happy to write the big check — now it's just about cashing it on the right guy.
Fans and media see a sound bite, while players see the relationship behind it, and those of us covering this team have a responsibility not to create a divide that isn't there. After a month of scorching takes about this core, it's easy to turn every quote into a feud. From the outside looking in, this looked like two people on the same page about running a business and competing for a championship together, and Yankees fans should take it as good news rather than another distraction.
If I'm Judge, I'm hanging up that phone call, then seeing the press conference and feeling like my owner has my back. Now the only question is whether the new ownership calculus turns that conversation into the pieces he asked for.

item.title: [New York Daily News] Yankees say they’ll ‘look into’ clubhouse culture criticisms, even as they downplay them
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips
item.description: In the hours, days and weeks since the Yankees’ latest postseason failure, their collective character has been dissected just as much as their disappointing play. Does there need to be more public accountability going forward? Does a team with a reputation for getting sloppy in the summer and in October pay enough attention to details? Have manager Aaron Boone and captain Aaron Judge fostered a country club atmosphere? Is every player truly bothered each time the pinstripers get embarrassed in t
item.content:encoded:
In the hours, days and weeks since the Yankees’ latest postseason failure, their collective character has been dissected just as much as their disappointing play.
Does there need to be more public accountability going forward? Does a team with a reputation for getting sloppy in the summer and in October pay enough attention to details? Have manager Aaron Boone and captain Aaron Judge fostered a country club atmosphere? Is every player truly bothered each time the pinstripers get embarrassed in the playoffs? Are there enough killers, enough grinders, in the room?
Are the current Yankees living up to the franchise’s storied standards? Do they have a culture problem?
All of these talking points have been raised since the Rays swept the Yankees in the ALDS and extended the Bombers’ title drought to 17 seasons. Some are fair, some are over the top, but they’ve nonetheless been topics of discussion in print, over the airwaves, and on social media.
Shortly after the Yankees were knocked out of the playoffs, the Daily News asked a member of the organization what they made of all that talk, especially the public perception of some that players are not held accountable. The source, an everyday presence in the clubhouse and dugout, was granted anonymity so that they could speak freely.
“Not sure honestly,” they replied. “Feels like a band aid or an easy solution to a complex situation. Players don’t respond to that type of feedback. The best accountability is ownership. Everyone is responsible for the shared environment that is created. Do we need more collective ownership… maybe?”
But, they added, “Inserting a few more alphas who run around policing everyone isn’t as impactful as you’d think. That’s not the secret sauce.”
Asked how the Yankees could take more collective ownership if key personnel don’t change — Boone and general manager Brian Cashman have since been retained — the source went on to say, “Speaking generally here, if you’re not getting the result you desire, I usually turn to the process first. Process can always improve. It’s never complete.”
To be clear, the Yankees did not lose the ALDS because of culture. They lost because they couldn’t field in Game 2, and because their lineup, missing an injured Judge, couldn’t hit throughout the series. Hal Steinbrenner certainly harped on the latter, chastising his offense’s “detrimental” performance on Wednesday while issuing his annual October votes of confidence to Boone and Cashman.
But the aforementioned source isn’t the only person who has criticized, questioned or hinted at intangible issues since the Yankees’ season ended.
Joe Girardi, Boone’s predecessor and less of a players’ manager, wondered if anyone is addressing the blunders the Yankees seem to make too often on “The Show” podcast. CC Sabathia, who played with and for Boone, said current Yankees “don’t know what that standard is… because there’s no one in there keeping that standard,” and that franchise greats aren’t around enough to uphold that on the “All The Smoke” podcast. And Anthony Rizzo, who played for the Yankees as recently as 2024 and remains tight with Judge, said it’s “insanity” for the Yankees to “keep doing the same thing every year” when championships aren’t being won on his own pod.
Keep in mind, those three are no longer in the Yankees’ clubhouse every day. But Judge and Cam Schlittler are, and both talked about standards after the Yankees’ were toppled by Tampa.
“There’s a standard to winning a championship,” Judge said. “It’s black and white. There’s no gray area. It’s every day you show up to work. Every little thing you do is, ‘Are you working toward a championship or you’re not?’ So I think that’s the biggest thing, is just everybody in the room understanding you gotta bring it every single day, especially here in New York. There’s no days off, and it just comes down to the little things and just preparing every single day like you’re preparing for a championship game.”
Schlittler, the impending AL Cy Young and one of the Yankees’ certified killers, added, “All the pieces are there. The talent’s there. I think we got the best talent in the league. But at the end of the day, we didn’t meet the standard that we have as an organization. It’s the second year in a row we gotta go home thinking about that. We just gotta be better.”
Schlittler also said that “it didn’t seem like we really showed up today” after the Yankees made four errors and misplayed a few other balls in a humiliating Game 2 ALDS loss.
On Wednesday, Steinbrenner said that he found that comment “concerning,” and that he wanted to talk to Schlittler about it to get a fuller sense of what he meant. The owner also indicated that he would talk it over with Judge, who already discussed a number of issues with Steinbrenner on Tuesday after he insinuated that the Yankees have not been “all in” enough during his career.
Meanwhile, Cashman said that he has spoken to a few ex-Yankees since the season ended. While he declined to say who he talked to and didn’t want to detail what he called “healthy, diplomatic, professional” chats, the revelation came in response to a question about the various remarks made by Girardi, Sabathia and Rizzo.
“I run to problems if they’re problems that do exist,” Cashman said. “It’s kind of my nature. I kind of put the hard hat on, and if something is amiss, then I’m going to try to address it or determine whether that really is amiss or not, so I proactively made phone calls based on a lot of the commentary that’s been out there, and I’ll continue to do so.”
Cashman also said that those conversations yielded “some healthy pointers,” but that there is always “noise” in the New York market. He added that he and each person he hit up agreed that “those issues aren’t why we’re losing those games.”
But does Cashman, now preparing for his 30th season as GM, believe there needs to be a culture change?
“We’re always trying to push culture,” he said. “We’re always trying to find higher ground, and that’s why, again, if something raises up the flagpole of, ‘Hey, there might be something here,’ let’s talk about it. Let’s address it. The one thing I’m very proud about is that, right or wrong, this organization is progressive. We are open-minded.”
“We’re going to look into it,” Steinbrenner chimed in.
That said, neither Cashman, Steinbrenner nor Boone seemed to think that holding players accountable in public more often was a change worth pursuing.
Boone and players — who can hear his postgame comments in the clubhouse — insist that tough talks do happen behind the scenes. And Boone does occasionally let it be openly known when he’s unhappy with someone, like when Jazz Chisholm Jr. played second base with a lollipop in his mouth in June.
But the skipper’s typical unwillingness to call out players for mistakes — or even objectively analyze poor performances at times — in front of cameras has long been a source of fan frustration.
“There is probably a time and place for that,” Boone, preparing for his 10th season as manager, acknowledged. “But generally speaking, to me, that’s not leadership. That’s me giving red meat to people who want to be upset with somebody.
“To me, when we have issues as a club or with an individual player or with something that popped up within a game, I address those things. We address those things man-to-man. Sometimes if we have to address something within the group, we do that.”
Steinbrenner’s father, George, often used the public square to motivate his players during his reign as owner, but the new boss said that heavy-handed tactic was for a “different generation,” and certainly not his style.
“My dad and I are different in that respect. I’m not convinced it would be effective anyway,” Steinbrenner said, noting that he pops into the Yankees’ clubhouse once or twice a homestand. “It’s just not the way I’m going to operate. I’m going to talk to them face-to-face.”
Cashman concurred, stating that private settings are “more appropriate” and “the most professional way” to handle things. He also said that he feels “there’s a built-in accountability, to the extreme, that’s around us every day” because of the spotlight that shines on the Yankees.
As for some of the comments made by his former players, Boone wasn’t sure what Rizzo was specifically referring to, but he pushed back on Sabathia’s suggestion that ex-Yankees don’t hang around enough. Boone described special assistant and five-time World Series champ Andy Pettitte as “a big part of our staff,” and he is always inviting legends of yesteryear to spring training.
Boone also believes that the Yankees had “a lot of the right ingredients” this year. Rebuking the public discourse, he called the team’s clubhouse “an absolute strength for us.”
Cashman, meanwhile, disputed the notion that the Yankees are lacking competitive nature as they embark on another offseason that started too soon.
“I do think our players are prepared,” the GM said. “I do think they are wired the right way. They care.”

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] Yankees news: Hal mum on labor
item.dc:creator: Nick Power
item.description: Daily News | Gary Phillips: ($) With the specter of a lockout looming over the 2027 season, Hal Steinbrenner was asked during his press conference Wednesday about hit thoughts on the owners’ salary cap proposal. The Yankees owner bristled at the questions, citing a desire to hold on discussing labor issues until after the World Series is complete while conceding that, as a member of the league’s labor policy committee, “I helped craft, one of many, the proposals that we have given at the bargain
item.content:encoded:
Daily News | Gary Phillips: ($) With the specter of a lockout looming over the 2027 season, Hal Steinbrenner was asked during his press conference Wednesday about hit thoughts on the owners’ salary cap proposal. The Yankees owner bristled at the questions, citing a desire to hold on discussing labor issues until after the World Series is complete while conceding that, as a member of the league’s labor policy committee, “I helped craft, one of many, the proposals that we have given at the bargaining table, and I support those proposals in their entirety.” Left unanswered is how a salary cap (and with it, potentially, a salary floor) could possibly give one of the league’s highest spenders a better chance to win, a refrain he returned to frequently as his top priority.
MLB.com | Shanthi Sepe-Chupuru: Congratulations are in order for Cody Bellinger, who took home his third Fielding Bible Award Thursday. The award, presented by Sports Info Solutions and voted on by a panel of experts, recognized him as the best defensive left fielder in all of baseball. Belli’s first two awards came back in 2019 with the Dodgers, when he was honored both for his work in right field and as a multi-position player. The 31-year-old’s 21 DRS tied for third in the majors at any position despite his missing nearly a month to injury.
The Athletic | Ian O’Connor: ($) The venerable former beat writer pens a pointed critique of Steinbrenner’s leadership, arguing the Yankees’ underperformance in October goes straight to the top. He contrasts the owner’s parsing of what makes a successful season with Derek Jeter’s more direct, “If we don’t win a championship, the season is a failure,” positing that Hal’s reticence to hold anyone to task publicly trickles down to a lack of accountability at all levels of the organization. O’Connor cites Jazz Chisholm Jr. as an example; after Aaron Boone indicated he addressed concerns with the second baseman behind the scenes in 2025, he had a dreadful ‘26 punctuated by taking the field with a lollipop in his mouth and contributing a head-scratching error in the first inning of Game 2 of the ALDS as the Yankees’ season slipped away yet again.
