item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees Birthday of the Day: Charlie Silvera
item.dc:creator: Matt Ferenchick
item.description: As far as non-stressful jobs in sports go, backup catcher to an established star would be a pretty good one to have. For nine years in New York, Charlie Silvera got to fill that role, and not just behind any old star — he was the backup to Yankees icon Yogi Berra. For his career in the Bronx, Silvera made less than 500 plate appearances, yet he still got to play a role on one of the most successful eras in the history of the most successful franchise. Charles Anthony Ryan "Charlie" Silvera Born:
item.content:encoded:
As far as non-stressful jobs in sports go, backup catcher to an established star would be a pretty good one to have. For nine years in New York, Charlie Silvera got to fill that role, and not just behind any old star — he was the backup to Yankees icon Yogi Berra. For his career in the Bronx, Silvera made less than 500 plate appearances, yet he still got to play a role on one of the most successful eras in the history of the most successful franchise.
Charles Anthony Ryan "Charlie" Silvera
Born: October 13, 1924 (San Francisco, CA)
Died: September 7, 2019 (Millbrae, CA)
Yankees Tenure: 1948-56
Silvera was born in San Francisco in 1924, going on to become one of a number of Yankees of that era to hail from the city. In his youth, he played sandlot baseball with fellow future Yankees Bobby Brown and Jerry Coleman. In 1942, he caught the eye of the Yankees, who signed him to a deal.
Silvera debuted in the minors as a 17-year old in 1942, playing for the Class D Wellsville (NY) Yankees as an outfielder. However after 75 games there that season, he joined the military, serving in the Air Force in World War II. Silvera would miss the entirety of the next three seasons while serving, although he did play on a military team during that time.
Upon returning to baseball, the Yankees converted Silvera into a catcher. He spent the next three seasons in the minors before earning a call-up to the Yankees late in the 1948 season. He appeared in four games, recording three hits in both of his first two games, and going 8-for-14 in total.
After that cameo, Silvera earned the Yankees' backup job for the 1949 season. He would spend the next nine seasons filling that role. The most games he ever appeared in a season came in his full debut year in '49. Starter Yogi Berra missed some time through injury and Silvera hit decently enough in his 58 games that season, putting up a .315 batting average and a .403 OBP. However, he was never going to fully replace the budding star in Berra, and never would. The Yankees also advanced to the 1949 World Series. Silvera came off the bench in Game 2 of the series, as Berra again had to exit due to injury. He went 0-for-2, as the Yankees lost that game but won the series. Despite playing in an era where the Yankees were winning and playing in the Fall Classic a lot, that was the only postseason appearance Silvera would ever make.
Over the next seven seasons, Silvera played in just 18, 18, 20, 42, 20, 14, and seven games respectively. Despite that, he would win five more World Series rings during his time with the Yankees. Opposing players would often try to trash talk Silvera for his lack of playing time, but the catcher was never bothered. He later said "the opposition would call me 'Jesse James, the payroll bandit.' I'd tell them, 'Go ahead and give it to me, but Yogi Berra tips me more than you make.'"
Having only appeared in 21 games over his last two seasons in the Bronx, the Yankees traded Silvera to the Cubs ahead of the 1957 season. Silvera put up a completely respectable — for a backup catcher — 86 OPS+ with the Yankees, he was just never going to replace Berra.
Upon going to the Cubs, Silvera was given the No. 8 that Berra wore in New York. He appeared in 26 games for Chicago that season, but struggled and missed time with injury. The Cubs released him after that season. Silvera played a couple more years in the minors but never made it back to the bigs, leaving the playing ranks after 1960.
Silvera stayed in baseball in various roles after his playing career ended. He joined former teammate Billy Martin on the coaching staffs of the Twins, Tigers, and Rangers when Martin was beginning his managerial career. He served as the bullpen coach for those teams, although Martin didn't bring him back to the Bronx when Martin went back there.
After coaching, Silvera got into scouting with the Cubs and Marlins. He received a seventh World Series ring for his work for the 1997 Marlins. He often came back for Yankees Old-Timers' Day but he did return to the San Francisco area in his later years, where he resided until his passing in 2019. Prior to his death, he had been the last surviving member of the Yankees dynasty to win five championships in a row from 1949-53.
Had he played in the modern era, Silvera very likely could've gone to another team in free agency to get more playing time. However, the rules at the time were what they were, and the Yankees were plenty happy to keep him around as a backup. Ending up with more than a hand's worth of World Series rings would be a nice consolation prize.
See more of the "Yankees Birthday of the Day" series here.

item.title: [Empire Sports Media] Paul Blackburn's next Yankees deal can't be based on ERA alone
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: I would try to bring Paul Blackburn back. I wouldn’t give him a long contract on the assumption that the Yankees just found a reliever who will run a 1.59 ERA every year. Those positions aren’t contradictory. Blackburn was excellent over 85 innings in 2026, and replacing that much useful work is an actual offseason expense. item.content:encoded:
I would try to bring Paul Blackburn back. I wouldn’t give him a long contract on the assumption that the Yankees just found a reliever who will run a 1.59 ERA every year.
Those positions aren’t contradictory. Blackburn was excellent over 85 innings in 2026, and replacing that much useful work is an actual offseason expense. His next deal still needs to reflect more than the most flattering number on his stat line.
What the Yankees would actually be paying for
Blackburn made 62 appearances, including two starts, and finished with a 1.08 WHIP. Opponents hit .195 against him. A pitcher who can give the club that much work without allowing many baserunners has obvious value, particularly when the bullpen needs more than three outs from somebody.
He also struck out 69 hitters and walked 33. His 7.31 strikeouts per nine innings were lower than his 7.85 rate in 2025, while his walks per nine rose from 2.77 to 3.49. The comparison uses his combined 2025 major-league season rather than his short Yankees stint alone.
That doesn’t erase his improvement. It does mean the ERA drop wasn’t accompanied by a jump in strikeouts or better walk control. I’d want the Yankees to price the full profile rather than treat the run prevention as a guarantee.
The runners already on base complicate it
Eleven of the 27 runners Blackburn inherited scored, or 40.7%. Those runs generally belong to the pitcher who put them on, so they don’t appear as earned runs on Blackburn’s record.
Twenty-seven runners is a small sample, and the number doesn’t tell us which bases were occupied, how many outs he inherited or what the defense did behind him. It would be unfair to declare him incapable of handling a jam from that figure alone. It would also be careless to ignore it when deciding whether to pay him like a top late-inning strikeout arm.
For me, the fit is a dependable pitcher who can start an inning, keep the game close and occasionally cover more than three outs. Bringing him back for that job leaves room to pursue a different type of reliever for situations where the Yankees need a strikeout with runners on.
Blackburn is headed toward free agency, so the team won’t get to set the price by itself. Another club may be willing to pay more for his innings and results. There’s no reported offer or bidding war behind my concern; it’s how I’d approach the decision before negotiations start.
A short multiyear deal would be reasonable if the cost still allows the Yankees to improve the rest of the bullpen. I’d be much less comfortable adding years just to beat another offer. Blackburn has earned a raise and a serious retention effort, but the Yankees need to pay for the job they want him to do, not buy the ERA and figure out the role afterward.
More about:New York Yankees

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are entering the offseason with plenty of questions surrounding their roster.
The Yankees were swept by the Tampa Bay Rays in the NLDS and now have some decisions to make. It is clear that they need to improve their roster if they hope to have more success in 2027.
One of the Yankees’ biggest decisions this offseason is about star infielder Jazz Chisholm Jr. The 28-year-old is a pending unrestricted free agent, and New York must decide if they want to bring him back. Given how shaky Chisholm’s 2026 season went, it would not be too surprising if both sides parted ways.
Yet, if the Yankees do not re-sign Chisholm, it would create a major hole in their infield. Due to this, the Yankees would need to find a replacement for him if he walked.
When looking at potential replacements for Chisholm, Atlanta Braves star Ozzie Albies stands out as a fascinating option. The 29-year-old would be a good player for New York to trade for if Chisholm does not return.
Braves’ Albies Is Creating Chatter in Rumor Mill & Yankees Should Target Him
Albies recently entered the rumor mill as a potential trade candidate. In a recent article for Bleacher Report, Joel Reuter named Albies one of baseball’s top offseason trade candidates to watch.
“Albies has spent his entire 10-year career with the Braves, tallying 25.7 WAR while earning four All-Star selections and winning two Silver Slugger awards,” Reuter wrote. “The surface-level power production was there once again, but he has posted a middling 88 OPS+ and .299 on-base percentage in 1,350 plate appearances the last two years, and the Braves could be ready to move on as part of a larger retooling.”
If the Braves make Albies available, the Yankees would be wise to target him. He has been a star throughout his career and could be a solid replacement for Chisholm. Due to this, he is among the players who the Yankees should have on their radar this offseason.
Albies Could Thrive With the Yankees
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – OCTOBER 04: Ozzie Albies #1 of the Atlanta Braves looks on prior to the game against the Los Angeles Dodgers in game two of the National League Division Series at Dodger Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Katelyn Mulcahy/Getty Images)
Albies would have the potential to thrive with the Yankees. He has been a very good player on the Braves for years now, so he has shown that he can handle playing for a top contender. Thus, it would not be too surprising if he had success on a team like the Yankees if acquired.
Albies is still an effective player at this point in his career, too. In 162 games last season for the Braves, he posted 22 home runs, 73 RBI, and a .237 batting average. He has also hit at least 22 home runs in five seasons of his MLB career. This included in 2023 when he hit a career-high 33 homers. With this, he could give the Yankees’ roster more pop.
Nevertheless, it will be interesting to see if the Yankees pursue Albies this offseason. If the Yankees let Chisholm walk and he signs elsewhere, Albies would make sense as a strong replacement for him.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees will have a chance to keep Jazz Chisholm Jr. this offseason.
He’s heading for free agency, but the Yankees aren’t shy about offering sizable contracts to players they want to keep.
The problem here is that the Yanks may decide they aren’t willing to pay Chisholm what he would want to stick around, which could result in him finding a new home in free agency.
This is actually Chisholm’s first foray into free agency. He was with the Miami Marlins to begin his career, and he came to the Yankees via trade.
Now, Chisholm has a chance to cash in. That payday might come from an unexpected place.
Jazz Chisholm Predicted Landing Spot
Bleacher Report’s Zachary D. Rymer wrote in a new article on Tuesday about where he thinks Chisholm might up, and it’s a fascinating move — the Los Angeles Angels.
Chisholm would be the Angels’ latest attempt to get Mike Trout to the playoffs for the first time in more than a decade.
“Chisholm could be in for a multi-year deal,” Rymer writes. “Yet after falling well short of his 50-50 goal and posting just 1.7 rWAR this year, the 28-year-old might be better off pursuing a one-year contract and reentering the market next winter. The Angels are just one of many teams that would have to be interested in such a deal. They are in need of help at the keystone, specifically, and upside on offense, generally. Chisholm can provide both, and some energy to boot. Depending on when the sale is finalized, signing Chisholm would also be a relatively low-risk way for Stan Kroenke to ingratiate himself with his new fanbase. Even if a one-year deal for Chisholm is valued at $20-plus million, he can afford it.”
The Angels have a fascinating outlook ahead with their new ownership, which clashes a decent amount with what their current team outlook feels like.
They’ve often been floated as a team that could trade experienced MLB players away, like shortstop Zach Neto.
But if the Angels go out and sign Chisholm, they’d certainly keep Neto to form a strong middle infield duo.
Why Yankees Would Let Jazz Chisholm Leave
For Chisholm to reach the Angels, of course, the Yankees would likely have to not offer him a reasonable new deal, because the second baseman has publicly seemed open to a return to the Bronx.
“I love it as a Yankee,” Chisholm said when the season ended.
Do they love him back?
“The Yankees have seemed ready to move on from Chisholm for months, and they have two potential replacements at second base in Anthony Volpe and Luis García Jr.,” Rymer writes.
The Yankees could certainly decide to just load up on talent and make it fit, but they may also choose to let Chisholm walk and focus their resources elsewhere.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees predicted to lose Jazz Chisholm Jr. to AL West team in free agency originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. made it clear. He prefers to stay with the New York Yankees.
"This is where I want to be. I love it as a Yankee," Chisholm said after New York's loss in Game 3 of the ALDS.
However, do the Yankees want to retain Chisholm? They could replace him at second base with Anthony Volpe.
Or the AL East club could move Luis Garcia Jr. back to middle infield and hope Ben Rice improves defensively at first base.
Regardless, Chisholm may be headed elsewhere this winter. Bleacher Report's Zachary D. Rymer predicts that the two-time All-Star will sign with the Los Angeles Angels.
"The Angels are just one of many teams that would have to be interested in such a deal. They are in need of help at the keystone, specifically, and upside on offense, generally. Chisholm can provide both, and some energy to boot," Rymer wrote.
Los Angeles could use another All-Star potential player or two in the lineup, and Chisholm is a consistent threat to hit 30 home runs and steal 30 bases a year.
He fell short of his expectations in 2026, hitting 19 homers with 41 steals after saying he wanted to have a 50-50 year.
If the Yankees are moving on from Chisholm, the Angels are a reasonable landing spot for the left-handed hitter.
"Depending on when the sale is finalized, signing Chisholm would also be a relatively low-risk way for Stan Kroenke to ingratiate himself with his new fanbase," Rymer added. "Even if a one-year deal for Chisholm is valued at $20-plus million, he can afford it."
Could this be the end of Chisholm's tenure in New York?

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Blue Jays linked to Yankees All-Star ahead of MLB offseason
item.dc:creator: Lou Landers
item.description: The MLB offseason could be a wild one, especially if there is a work stoppage, and the Toronto Blue Jays could be looking for ways to add more offense before it happens. YES of NO: Jazz Chisholm Jr. to the Blue Jays? Mark Feinsand lists Toronto as one of the potential suitors for the Yankees second baseman. https://t.co/UOFyNznsee — SleeperBlueJays (@SleeperBlueJays) October 12, 2026 One intriguing possibility involves New York Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr., with MLB.com's Mark Feinsa
item.content:encoded:
The MLB offseason could be a wild one, especially if there is a work stoppage, and the Toronto Blue Jays could be looking for ways to add more offense before it happens.
YES of NO: Jazz Chisholm Jr. to the Blue Jays? Mark Feinsand lists Toronto as one of the potential suitors for the Yankees second baseman. https://t.co/UOFyNznsee
— SleeperBlueJays (@SleeperBlueJays) October 12, 2026
One intriguing possibility involves New York Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr., with MLB.com's Mark Feinsand identifying Toronto as a potential landing spot for the two-time All-Star.
Why Chisholm could make sense for Toronto
Jul 19, 2026; Bronx, New York, USA; New York Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. (13) and center fielder Trent Grisham (12) celebrate after defeating the Los Angeles Dodgers at Yankee Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Brad Penner-Imagn Images
There is an obvious argument for the Blue Jays pursuing Chisholm. Toronto finished last in MLB in runs scored in 2026, producing only 648 runs. Adding a dynamic left-handed hitter with Chisholm's power and speed could give the lineup a much-needed jolt.
Chisholm did not duplicate his 2025 production, when he became a 30-30 player, but he still provided plenty of value in 2026. He hit .231 with 19 home runs, 55 RBIs and 41 stolen bases over 137 games while producing 3.5 fWAR. His 41 stolen bases ranked third in the American League.
The Blue Jays also have a potential opening at second base. Ernie Clement can handle the position, but Feinsand noted that Clement struggled significantly down the stretch, posting a .442 OPS across August and September. Toronto general manager Ross Atkins has also indicated that Clement will have to earn his starting role next spring.
That could create an opportunity for Chisholm to step into the lineup while allowing Clement to take on a valuable super-utility role.
Why Toronto should think twice
Mar 25, 2026; San Francisco, California, USA; New York Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. (13) slides safely into third base against the San Francisco Giants in the second inning at Oracle Park. Mandatory Credit: Cary Edmondson-Imagn Images
The biggest question is whether Chisholm would be worth the financial commitment required to bring him to Toronto.
Despite his talent, the 29-year-old is coming off a down offensive season. He struck out 157 times in 532 plate appearances and posted a 29.5% strikeout rate, placing him in the bottom 10% of MLB in that category. His 30.9% whiff rate also ranked in the bottom 10%.
Additionally, there are questions about his injury history and how much money Toronto should commit to him following a season in which his offensive production declined.
Feinsand's analysis suggests a three-to-four-year contract worth roughly $20 million annually could be a reasonable range, although the final price will depend heavily on how the free-agent market develops.
For Toronto, the upside is obvious: Chisholm brings speed, athleticism, power and a left-handed bat to a lineup that badly needs more production.
The risk is equally clear.

item.content:encoded:
Should the New York Yankees consider making a blockbuster trade for San Francisco Giants‘ infielder Matt Chapman?
After a disappointing 2026 season that concluded with an early exit in the MLB playoffs, the offseason is now for the Yanks.
Entering the offseason, the expectation is that the Yankees will look a lot different in certain areas of the diamond. One of those areas could be third base, where the Yankees really struggled offensively in 2026.
Matt Chapman stands out as a possible trade candidate, and a player New York should consider trading for.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Urged to Part Ways with 7X MLB All-Star in Offseason Move
Yankees Trade Package for Matt Chapman Revealed
In this hypothetical trade package, the New York Yankees land Giants’ $151 million infielder Matt Chapman for two players: RHP Clarke Schmidt and LHP prospect Kyle Carr.
Recently, BR.com’s Joel Reuter named Matt Chapman as one of 25 possible offseason trade candidates, and with the Yankees’ need for a left side of the field player, rumors are likely to spin in for the Yankees to acquire Chapman.
“While Rafael Devers, Willy Adames and Jung Hoo Lee are generally viewed as unavailable or immovable, Chapman is the one high-priced veteran the Giants might be able to flip, using last year’s Nolan Arenado trade as a blueprint of sorts. He had season-ending core muscle and hernia surgery in August, but is expected to be ready for the start of next season.”
In 2026, Chapman hit 7 home runs, 18 doubles, and posted an OPS+ of 97 in 84 games.
Injuries were clearly part of Chapman’s 2026 season, but that shouldn’t stop the Yankees from acquiring a consistent Gold Glove shortstop, and considering Clarke Schmidt doesn’t really have a role in the Yankees’ rotation, he could be expendable.
Chapman is tied to a six-year, $151 million contract, but he’s consistently been a 4.0+ bWAR player, which makes the contract a reasonable one to take on. His bWAR was 2.7 in 2026, but in only 84 games, that’s a very solid number. For comparison, Ryan McMahon (the Yankees’ primary third baseman) posted a bWAR of 0.0 in 124 games played.
More MLB on Heavy: Dave Roberts Sounds Off on Will Smith After Brewers Loss

item.content:encoded:
Decisions, decisions.
For the New York Yankees this offseason, the front office has several decisions to make regarding retaining players who are set to hit the open market in free agency.
One of those big decisions for Brian Cashman and company is with 7X MLB All-Star infielder Paul Goldschmidt, who has indicated he would like to play in the 2027 season, but will it be with the New York Yankees?
More MLB on Heavy: Anthony Volpe Sounds Off On New York Yankees with 2-Word Message
Yankees Predicted to Let Paul Goldschmidt Walk in Free Agency
Paul Goldschmidt is coming off a solid campaign with the Yankees in 2026.
The 7x All-Star batted .252 with 18 home runs, 87 hits, 52 RBI, and an OPS+ of 111.
However, FanSided.com's Adam Weinrib recently urged that the Yankees should part ways with Goldschmidt:
"The Yankees have collected DH/first basemen like talismans all season, rotating Ben Rice and Luis Garcia Jr. and likely needing room for some Aaron Judge first base reps next year. Goldy has been a consummate professional. Every time you thought he was done contributing, he found an additional layer. But he's 39 years old. The Yankees value flexibility and probably don't want to roster a lefties-only first base backup."
Aside from Goldschmidt, the Yankees will also have decisions to make with players such as Jazz Chisholm Jr., Trent Grisham, and David Bednar/Paul Blackburn.
It could be an entirely new-looking Yankees squad in 2027, but speaking to Goldschmidt's free agency status, it feels like a toss-up if he will be back with the team or not. Ben Rice has emerged as the everyday first baseman for New York, and if that means Goldschmidt would get significantly less at-bats, why should Cashman commit to him for a one-year pact?
Perhaps the 39-year-old infielder would rather sign with a team like the St. Louis Cardinals in a reunion deal, which would allow him to see some time as a platoon DH.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Urged to be Cautious with Potential Aaron Boone Replacement
Paul Goldschmidt is Likely Headed for Hall of Fame
While his production has slowed a little bit over recent seasons, Goldschmidt is likely headed for the Hall of Fame.
Across 16 years and 2179 games played, the 39 y/o has 390 home runs, 490 doubles, 1284 RBI, and a lifetime batting average of .286.
He was once considered the best first baseman in all of MLB, which led to the Yankees bringing him in before the 2025 season, and he's found some resurgence in his career since joining New York.
It will be very interesting to see the approach that the Yankees take during his free agency negotiations, and if the front office considers bringing him back.
More MLB on Heavy: Dave Roberts Sounds Off on Will Smith After Brewers Loss

item.content:encoded:
It's time for vote for the 2026 Hank Aaron Award, an honor that recognizes the most outstanding regular season offensive performer in each League. At last year’s All-Star Game in Atlanta, MLB celebrated the 51st anniversary of Hank Aaron’s historic 715th record-breaking home run with a special in-game presentation. This year marks the 27th anniversary of the Hank Aaron Award’s introduction, which was established to honor the momentous milestone.
The Hank Aaron Award winners will be announced live from The Chelsea at The Cosmopolitan of Las Vegas on Wednesday, Nov. 11 at 9 p.m. ET/6 p.m. PT during a special presentation at the MLB Awards, which will be aired live on MLB Network for a fourth consecutive year. Three-time Hank Aaron Award winner Shohei Ohtani (2023-25) is among this year’s finalists. Also among this year’s finalists are a pair of MLB Develops alumni, including Jordan Walker (DREAM Series and Breakthrough Series in 2019) and Bobby Witt Jr. (States Play in 2018).
2026 HANK AARON AWARD FINALISTS
American League
Pete Alonso - Baltimore Orioles 
Yordan Alvarez - Houston Astros 
Randy Arozarena - Seattle Mariners 
Junior Caminero - Tampa Bay Rays 
Willson Contreras - Boston Red Sox 
Yandy Díaz - Tampa Bay Rays
Riley Greene - Detroit Tigers 
Ben Rice - New York Yankees 
Miguel Vargas - Chicago White Sox 
Bobby Witt Jr. - Kansas City Royals 
National League
CJ Abrams - Washington Nationals
Jake Bauers - Milwaukee Brewers
Pete Crow-Armstrong - Chicago Cubs
Elly De La Cruz - Cincinnati Reds
Shohei Ohtani - Los Angeles Dodgers
Matt Olson - Atlanta Braves
Kyle Schwarber - Philadelphia Phillies
Sal Stewart - Cincinnati Reds
Fernando Tatis Jr. - San Diego Padres
Jordan Walker - St. Louis Cardinals
A committee of MLB.com journalists reviewed the top offensive statistics, accomplishments, and performances of the regular season to determine the ten finalists for each league. MLB legends and past recipients of the prestigious award comprise the renowned panel that each cast votes for their choices for the honor. The distinguished group includes: 2006 and 2009 Hank Aaron Award winner Derek Jeter; 2005 and 2016 Hank Aaron Award winner David Ortiz; 2003 and 2009 Hank Aaron Award winner Albert Pujols; Ken Griffey Jr.; Chipper Jones; Pedro Martínez; John Smoltz; Johnny Bench; Craig Biggio; and Eddie Murray.
Fans also have the opportunity to cast their vote on who should receive this distinguished award by voting from the list of finalists in each the American League and National League through MLB.com/aaron. The voting window begins today at noon and runs through Monday, Oct. 12 at 11:59 a.m. ET.
The Hank Aaron Award was introduced in 1999 to honor the 25th Anniversary of Aaron breaking Babe Ruth’s all-time home run record, and, at that time, was the first major award introduced by Major League Baseball in more than 25 years.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Aaron Boone's Luis Garcia Jr. comments hint at a confusing Yankees grand plan

item.content:encoded:
Luis Garcia Jr. proved in 2026 that he's an intriguing piece for the New York Yankees' future, at least in the short term. The 26-year-old hits free agency following the 2027 season, so the Yankees will get one more look to see if they want to sign him long-term.
The issue with Garcia isn't his talent, but rather his fit on the roster. In his desperate quest to augment the offense at the trade deadline, Brian Cashman created a logjam of sorts. In the field, Garcia Jr. shares the same position as break out star Ben Rice. While one of them can DH, it's not an ideal solution.
New York has Giancarlo Stanton under contract for 2027, and should also give strong consideration to at least semi-regular DH days for Aaron Judge moving forward. There are only so many at-bats to go around.
Aaron Boone has a solution. Just change Garcia Jr.'s position.
“Obviously, an infielder in his [Garcia Jr.'s] past, and feel like that could even be in play, you know, moving forward in coming years,” Boone said via Brendan Kuty of The Athletic.
What Boone is referring to is Garcia Jr.'s history as a shortstop-turned-second baseman. Garcia Jr. never really stuck at short, playing just 70 career games at the position, with the majority coming in 2022. Since then, he has been a second baseman almost exclusively until this year.
With Jazz Chisholm Jr. hitting free agency and seemingly destined to leave, it seems like a perfect fit to just slide Garcia Jr. over and cross that need off the offseason list. The problem is that Garcia Jr. moved to first because he was miserable defensively at the keystone.
Trying Luis Garcia Jr. out at another position isn't out of the question, but the Yankees need a backup plan
Solving the offensive logjam and finding a way to get Garcia Jr., Rice, Judge, and possibly Stanton into the lineup at the same time is important, but it all falls apart if Garcia Jr. gives back everything he produces in the field. We've seen how badly New York's shoddy defense can derail their plans, with Game 2 of the ALDS against the Tampa Bay Rays serving as exhibits A through Z.
Simply put, the Yankees' defense needs to get better, not worse. But notice how Boone didn't name a position for Garcia Jr.? He just mentioned that they might be able to try some different things out due to the former Washington National's perceived versatility.
That's led to some fans on social media clamoring for New York to give him a shot at third base. While not exactly the same, range hasn't been an issue for Garcia Jr. at first, with him posting three outs above average and two defensive runs saved at the cold corner this year. The question will be whether or not his arm can hold up there.
The Yankees are unlikely to spend big at third base. Ryan McMahon has been a complete black hole at third base, as few hitters in the league can match his ineptitude at getting on base and avoiding strikeouts. Defense was once his calling card, but that fell off in 2026, too, with him recording -3 DRS and 0 OAA. He's owed $16 million in 2027, the final year of his contract. We can only hope that the Yankees decide to cut bait and just eat that money over the winter.
The problem is Garcia Jr. likely needs a platoon partner, and given that this kind of position change would be a roll of the dice, they'd need to find someone who not only hits right-handed, but could move into the position full-time and not be completely over his head should the experiment fail. Unfortunately, the third base free-agent market is pretty bare.
At the end of the day, this is an intriguing option for the Yankees, but not one that they can bank on. Putting all of their chips on Garcia Jr. playing a position that he has either proven he already isn't good at or has never played before, without a reasonable backup plan, is inviting an unnecessarily combustible situation.

item.description: The biggest question the New York Yankees are facing this offseason is what will happen with their manager, Aaron Boone. In the immediate aftermath of the Yankees being eliminated from the MLB playoffs, there haven't been any official reports about Boone's status with the organization, but the rumor mill is certainly swirling, and there's plenty of speculation regarding candidates who could replace Aaron Boone. One potential option is Don Mattingly, who is extremely familiar with the Yankees org
item.content:encoded:
The biggest question the New York Yankees are facing this offseason is what will happen with their manager, Aaron Boone.
In the immediate aftermath of the Yankees being eliminated from the MLB playoffs, there haven't been any official reports about Boone's status with the organization, but the rumor mill is certainly swirling, and there's plenty of speculation regarding candidates who could replace Aaron Boone.
One potential option is Don Mattingly, who is extremely familiar with the Yankees organization, being that he played in Pinstripes for 10+ seasons.
However, in a recent think piece by FanSided.com's Pat Ragazzo, the MLB writer notes that adding Mattingly to the staff may not be the move that solves all issues for the Yankees.
More MLB on Heavy: Anthony Volpe Sounds Off On New York Yankees with 2-Word Message
MLB Writer Urges Yankees to be Cautious with Don Mattingly as Boone Replacement
Again, there hasn't been any indication that Aaron Boone won't be the Yankees skipper in 2027, but fans have steadily been calling for him to be fired due to the fact that this recent ALDS loss felt very synonymous with how the Yankees have been eliminated in recent seasons (aside from the 2024 World Series run).
"Despite having a successful playing career with the Yankees, Mattingly isn't as well equipped as Boone to be managing in New York. Boone has extensive managerial experience in New York, and Mattingly only lasted five seasons with the Dodgers in Los Angeles. If Mattingly came back to the Bronx as the skipper and faltered, it could hurt his legacy with the Yankees."
Ragazzo also notes that since Aaron Boone has one year left on his contract, he's likely to stay with the Yankees for at least one more season.
And as for Mattingly, he's still in the running to become the full-time manager for the Phillies, although Philadelphia is expected to have an open managerial search.
Mattingly spent his entire 14-year career with the Yankees and was a six-time MLB All-Star and former AL MVP.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Make Interesting Roster Move Following MLB Playoff Elimination
What's Next for New York Yankees if Aaron Boone Remains the Skipper?
It's hard to fault Aaron Boone for the lack of offense the Yankees displayed against the Rays, but I think most of the New York fans are displeased with the same hamster-wheel cycle that has been the Aaron Boone experiment since he was hired.
However, if he is to remain the Yankees skipper, Brian Cashman is likely to make a handful of moves that will make this Yankees roster look a whole lot different once 2027 rolls around.
Cashman has decisions to make with players such as Paul Goldschmidt, Trent Grisham, Jazz Chisholm Jr., and a few pitchers.
The good news for the Yankees is that their starting rotation will remain intact, and Aaron Judge should play (if all goes well) a lot more than he did in 2026.
The Yankees remain at the forefront of major storylines in MLB as the offseason nears, and Aaron Boone's status will be a well-documented topic until a final decision is made on his future with the organization.

item.title: [MLB.com] Where could Jazz Chisholm Jr. land in free agency?

item.content:encoded:
Position: Second baseman
Team: New York Yankees
“I just can’t help but get that gut feeling,” Chisholm said at the start of Spring Training. “It’s going to be an amazing year.”
Chisholm didn’t approach his lofty goals, hitting 19 home runs with 55 RBIs and a career-high 41 stolen bases, ranking third in the American League in that last category. Defensive metrics were mixed on Chisholm; he posted 15 outs above average, ranking in the 98th percentile of MLB in the defensive metric, though he was a -6 in defensive runs saved.
The two-time All-Star struggled against left-handed pitching, posting a .218/.269/.381 slash line against southpaws, a steep drop from his stats against righties (.238/.331/.407).
This year’s free-agent market offers some options at second base, with Chisholm, Brandon Lowe and Luis Arraez heading up a class that also includes Mauricio Dubón and Gleyber Torres. Chisholm is the most dynamic offensive player of that group, but the number of available players means clubs seeking help at second base will have choices.
One factor working to Chisholm’s advantage: his age. He is three years younger than Lowe, Seiya Suzuki and Randy Arozarena, three of the top hitters available this offseason. Chisholm is also the lone player in that group to post an fWAR of 3.0 or higher in each of the past three seasons.
Let’s take a look at how Chisholm’s offseason might play out:
POTENTIAL SUITORS
YANKEES
Chisholm has been productive during his time in New York, but it feels like the Yankees are ready to move on with one of their other options at second base. Luis Garcia Jr. has played the majority of his games at second base during his career, so he could move back there in 2027, or the Yanks could put Anthony Volpe at second base after he proved the ability to play there this season. The Yankees have options, though bringing back Chisholm remains one of them.
TIGERS
Detroit has an opening at second base with Torres headed for free agency for a second straight season, opening a potential spot for Chisholm. The Tigers like Hao-Yu Lee, who offers versatility and could serve as a super utility player. The lineup could use a left-handed bat and an injection of speed, making Chisholm a potential fit.
BLUE JAYS
Toronto could easily plug Ernie Clement into its second-base spot, but Clement stumbled down the stretch this season, posting a .442 combined OPS in August and September. General manager Ross Atkins has said publicly that Clement will have to earn his spot next spring, but could the Blue Jays look to add a new second baseman via free agency and utilize Clement as a super utility man? Given that Toronto ranked last in the Majors in runs scored (648), the lineup certainly could use a jolt somewhere.
ANGELS
Los Angeles ranked 29th in the Majors in runs scored (655) and last in OPS (.679), making the offense an obvious priority this offseason. Second base was one of the biggest problem areas for the Angels, whose .620 OPS at the position ranked last in the AL and 28th overall in the Majors. With Stan Kroenke taking over, signing a two-time All-Star like Chisholm could be a big splash for new ownership to make.
PADRES
San Diego could use some left-handed power, slugging only .384 from that side of the plate in 2026, which ranked 23rd in the Majors. Second base is one of the logical spots for the Padres to upgrade, as they could move Jake Cronenworth to first base to open the spot for somebody such as Chisholm. As for the swag that stood out like a sore thumb at times with the Yankees, Chisholm would fit in perfectly with the Padres’ roster.
REDS
Baseball-wise, there might not be a better fit for Chisholm than the Reds, who ranked 29th in the Majors with a .608 OPS at second base and 27th overall with a .693 OPS against right-handed pitching. The biggest question is whether Cincinnati will be willing to give Chisholm a multi-year deal, though it’s conceivable that he could seek a one-year “prove it” deal with an eye toward testing free agency again a year from now.
BUYER BEWARE
If there is one negative aspect to Chisholm’s offensive game, it’s his tendency to swing and miss. Chisholm ranked in the 13th percentile of MLB in whiff percentage (30.9%) and the bottom 10 percent in strikeout percentage, striking out 157 times in 532 plate appearances (29.5%). In his 30-30 season of 2025, he also ranked in the bottom 10 percent in both numbers.
EXECUTIVE TAKE
“He's an interesting case, because if you look at Jazz from an age and WAR standpoint, he'd appear to be a pretty decent candidate to receive a qualifying offer entering his age-29 season. A 3.5 fWAR for a second baseman with some power would make the roughly $23 million [qualifying offer] pretty palatable. But I think if you dig in a little more and look at his WRC+ and overall trend, it might have been his worst offensive season since 2021. Layer in the Yankees getting pretty poor value from [Trent] Grisham this year, who they just QO'd, and it seems likelier that they won't end up doing so with Jazz.
“From a free-agent standpoint, he's been a 3-4 WAR guy for three years now, and he’s still fairly young, so a three- to four-year deal at roughly $20 million [average annual value] would seem pretty fair -- which again begs the question on if a qualifying offer isn't actually reasonable value for him. I think it's safe to say he won't get anything close to what he was reportedly looking for [eight to 10 years, $35 million AAV], according to that report from earlier this season.”
FOR COMP'S SAKE
Only two second basemen have signed nine-figure free-agent deals: Robinson Cano (10 years, $240 million with the Mariners in December 2013) and Marcus Semien (seven-year, $175 million with the Rangers in December 2021). DJ LeMahieu’s six-year, $90 million deal with the Yankees before the 2021 season is next on the list, though LeMahieu had a career bWAR of 25 at the time, while Chisholm’s is 14.2. Chisholm’s three-year output should put him in line for a multi-year deal, though he could also look for a one-year deal to boost his free-agent value even further and test the market again next offseason.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] 100 Years ago Cards Became World Series Champs by Besting Babe Ruth
item.dc:creator: John Denton
item.description: Roundtable Sports' John Denton details the Cardinals' first World Series victory 100 years ago this weekend in the 1926 World Series over the New York Yankees. One hundred years ago this weekend, when the St. Louis Cardinalsbeat the Yankees 3-2 before 38,093 fans at Yankee Stadium in Game 7, the Cardswon the first of their 11 World Series crowns in the unlikeliest of ways. Babe Ruth, arguably the most celebrated slugger in the historyof baseball, was thrown out by Cardinals catcher Bob O'Farrell
item.content:encoded:
Roundtable Sports' John Denton details the Cardinals' first World Series victory 100 years ago this weekend in the 1926 World Series over the New York Yankees.
One hundred years ago this weekend, when the St. Louis Cardinalsbeat the Yankees 3-2 before 38,093 fans at Yankee Stadium in Game 7, the Cardswon the first of their 11 World Series crowns in the unlikeliest of ways.
Babe Ruth, arguably the most celebrated slugger in the historyof baseball, was thrown out by Cardinals catcher Bob O'Farrell while trying toswipe second base. When player/manager Rogers Hornsby applied the tag, it gave St.Louis its first-ever championship by a professional sports franchise.
Even today, 100 years later, it is the only World Series toend with a base runner to get caught trying to steal a base.
1926 World's Series
Game 7
Oct 10 1926
BOTTOM 9TH
Ruth on first after walking...
RUTH BREAKS FOR SECOND!
O'FARRELL FIRES TO HORNSBY—
THE TAG IS ON HIM!
OUT! OUT AT SECOND!
BABE RUTH IS CAUGHT STEALING!
THE GAME IS OVER!
THE ST. LOUIS CARDINALS ARE CHAMPIONS OF THE WORLD! pic.twitter.com/8UFij1rmwn
— 1926 Cardinals (@CardsManager) October 10, 2026
The Cardinals' first World Series win ushered in an era ofgreatness for the franchise. Between 1926 and 1934, the Cards won five NationalLeague pennants and three World Series titles. Today, 100 years later, theCardinals added eight more World Series trophies, and their 11 World Seriescrowns still rank as the most in National League history.
Incredibly, there were 13 Hall of Famers who took part inthe seven-game series, which was ranked by ESPN in 2020 as the 10thgreatest World Series ever played. The Cardinals boasted Hall of Famers GoverCleveland Alexander, Him Bottomley, Chick Hafey, Jesse Haines, Billy Southworth(inducted as a manager) and Hornsby, whose availability in the series was putin doubt when his mother died on Sept. 29. Reportedly, Hornsby was conflictedabout playing and managing in the series, but a telegram from his uncle convincedhim that his mother would have wanted him to play, per the Philadelphia Inquirer.Hornsby reported decided to play and manager when his mother's burial wasdelayed until after the completion of the World Series.
The Yankees were led by Hall of Famers Earle Combs, LouGehrig, Waite Hoyt, Tony Lazzeri, Herb Pennock, manager Miller Huggins and Ruth,who smashed four home runs in the World Series.
Trailing 3-2 in the series, the Cardinals won Game 6 10-2behind a 13-hit attack offensively and the pitching of Cleveland Alexander. Alexanderwas the choice to close out Game 7 as well, earning his first save in thatdeciding game.
Trailing 1-0 in Game 7 after Ruth's blast into the rightfield bleachers, the Cardinals responded with three runs in the top of thefourth inning. The first run scored on an error by Yankees left fielder BobMeusel. Then, infielder Tommy Thevenow lined a two-run single to Ruth in rightfield to put the Cardinals ahead to stay. Incredibly, all three Cardinals' runsoff Hoyt were unearned because of two Yankees errors.
After the Yankees got within 3-2, Hornsby made the decisionto go to Cleveland Alexander, the Game 6 winner to close out Game 7. According "TheBaseball Biography Project" published by the Society for American BaseballResearch, Hornsby told Cleveland to limit his alcohol consumption following hiscomplete-game outing in Game 6 because he might be needed to close out Game 7.
With two outs in the ninth inning, Cleveland Alexander wiselypitched around Ruth for the slugger's fourth walk of the game. That meant hehad to pitch to Meusel – the outfielder whose error kick-started St. Louis' three-runfourth inning – even though the Yankees' outfielder had doubled and tripled offCleveland Alexander in Game 6. Gehrig, the famed "Iron Horse," was in theon-deck circle.
Debate raged for years where Huggins put on a hit-and-runcall that was missed by Meusel, but years later Ruth claimed he was just tryingto get into scoring position, according to Jonathan Eig, author of LuckiestMan: The Life and Death of Lou Gehrig.
According to Glenn Stout, author of 100 Years of YankeesBaseball, Hornsby had this to say about tagging out Ruth to end the WorldSeries: "(Ruth) didn't say a word. He didn't even look around or up at me. Hejust picked himself up and walked away."

Former MLB star Gary Sheffield’s son, Gary Sheffield Jr., jokingly asked whether Judge plans
item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees legends Derek Jeter and CC Sabathia reacted strongly after Aaron Judge & Co’s ALDS elimination by the Tampa Bay Rays extended their World Series drought to 17 years. Though Judge wasn’t available this postseason because of a calf injury, the Yankees legends said the veteran lacks the ability to create the right clubhouse atmosphere, citing it as a reason for repeated postseason failures.
Former MLB star Gary Sheffield’s son, Gary Sheffield Jr., jokingly asked whether Judge plans to ignore all those comments from the franchise’s past legends.
“I wonder if Aaron Judge plans to block CC, Jorge, Jeter, A-Rod, and Rizzo on here for saying the clubhouse has become a joke? Asking for a friend 🤣 Not wrong, just early. My bad, bro @TheJudge44,” Sheffield Jr. wrote on X.
Judge sounded serious enough in his reaction to the Yankees’ early postseason elimination. The Yankees captain wants the front office to be aggressive in the offseason so they can do better next year and finally give New York its first World Series since Jeter & Co. won it all in 2009.
What Each Former Yankee Said After Aaron Judge & Co. Came Up Short in October
Former Yankees Cy Young winner CC Sabathia argued the team no longer has veterans to enforce the Yankees’ traditional standards, especially since manager Joe Girardi’s departure in 2017. He said former leaders such as Jorge Posada, Jeter and Mariano Rivera are no longer around the clubhouse to set the example.
“Jorge’s not around,” Sabathia said on Saturday’s episode of the “ALL THE SMOKE BASEBALL” podcast. “Derek is sitting on the Fox desk. Mo is somewhere selling hot sauce. You know what I’m saying? These dudes need to be around the clubhouse. They need to be in Tampa in spring training. Like, that was the standard. That’s how the standard is set. And those guys ain’t around no more. It’s completely different.”
Advertisement
Meanwhile, Jeter criticized the team’s repeated mistakes, particularly baserunning errors on Fox’s pregame show (per MLB.com). Alex Rodriguez spoke about accountability and the need for strong action when repeated mistakes are made.
A big question mark is also brewing about whether Judge needs to take the initiative and create a competitive atmosphere in the clubhouse.

item.content:encoded:
After failing to acquire a catcher at the trade deadline in August, the New York Yankees can revisit improvements behind the plate during the offseason.
The Yankees' catching room was a disaster for the first half, as Austin Wells suddenly declined into the worst qualified hitter in baseball while J.C. Escarra and Ali Sanchez contributed next to nothing. Wells noticeably improved in the second half, but Sanchez remained a massive liability both at and behind the plate.
Although Wells' productive finish to the season effectively saved his job, it's become extremely clear that the Yankees cannot rely on him catching every single day. The 27-year-old was behind the plate in 122 of the Bronx Bombers' 161 games this year, marking the second consecutive season he caught that many games.
In contrast, Wells caught 110 games in 2024 and had Jose Trevino as a serviceable backup. He finished as a finalist for AL Rookie of the Year that season.
Wells is not the problem with the Yankees' catching woes: rather, it's the lack of depth behind him. His increased workload over the past two seasons are the result of suboptimal backup catchers, and it's resulted in his offense declining. Even with his solid second half, it's more likely for Wells to sustain that form if he has a much better backup to share some of the load with.
The good news for both Wells and the Yankees is there are 14 catchers hitting free agency this winter, with a majority of them being right-handed hitters as well. Compared to the trade deadline, it should be much easier to find a backstop to platoon with Wells or even share the starting role with him.
Here are the four best options for the Yankees to pursue.
Ryan Jeffers
This one is obvious, especially since the Yankees have been linked to Ryan Jeffers in trade rumors before. Jeffers will be the best available catcher in free agency, and even though he was limited to 92 games with a fractured hamate bone, the 29-year-old had one of his best offensive seasons by hitting .256/.353/.461 with 14 home runs and a 128 wRC+.
Jeffers' defense is still a work in progress, but his framing has improved over the years and having a previous connection with Tanner Swanson, the Yankees' catching coordinator, should help him improve further. Additionally, Jeffers has mashed southpaws in his career to the tune of a .270/.365/.464 slash line, making him a perfect platoon partner with Wells.
Due to Jeffers' experience as a starter, it's very feasible for the Yankees to have him and Wells share the workload over the course of a season. While it may come at the cost of some playing time, Wells would be able to concentrate more on maintaining his hitting prowess and would take less of a beating behind the plate by having Jeffers as a proven option with him.
Carson Kelly
There's no guarantee that Carson Kelly hits the market due to his mutual option with the Chicago Cubs for 2027. However, those kind of options rarely come to fruition due to either the player or team declining it, so the Yankees should expect Kelly to be available and show great interest in him.
An outstanding platoon bat, the 32-year-old veteran hit lefties at a .298/.375/.496 clip and a 143 wRC+. Kelly's defense was also respectable, being especially adept at ABS challenges much like Wells is.
Kelly handled a starter's workload with the Cubs over the past two seasons, so getting him would cut into Wells' playing time. But given his veteran presence and mastery against southpaws, that's a good thing.
Kyle Higashioka
Just like Kelly, Kyle Higashioka has a mutual option for 2027. Yet it wouldn't hurt the Yankees to pursue a reunion with the 36-year-old.
Higgy's familiarity with the organization and Gerrit Cole should make it easy for him to adjust towards handling a new pitching staff. And while he is still a below-average hitter, he's still capable of going yard once in a while; Higashioka registered a .420 slugging percentage in the three seasons since leaving the Bronx.
Compared to Jeffers and Kelly, Higashioka has far less upside and would still leave Wells with the lion's share of catching duties. But having a major league veteran like him is absolutely better than having a minor league journeyman like Ali Sanchez as the backup.
Gary Sanchez
Hear me out: a reunion with Gary Sanchez to back up Wells would be a solid offensive upgrade.
While his defense is still not great, the 33-year-old has been productive with the Milwaukee Brewers this season, largely due to significantly improved plate discipline. In 275 plate appearances, Sanchez has countered a .209 batting average with a .349 on-base percentage, drawing 46 walks and submitting a chase rate of just 23%. The Kraken's trademark power is still there, with nearly half of his hits going for extra bases (including 12 home runs).
Having a right-handed power threat like Sanchez, alongside his improved on-base skills, would make the Yankees' catching tandem significantly more threatening offensively. And even if Sanchez's defense was often a point of contention when he played in New York in the past, he was a starter back then; using him as a backup to Wells gives the Bronx Bombers an option to prioritize either offense or defense in a given game.
Sanchez also has a mutual option for 2027, but that is unlikely to be exercised by the Brewers.
Joe Najarian is a writer for Yankees On SI, having previously covered the Yankees both for SI and additional sites since 2023. He also served as Deputy Editor for the Yankees, Mets and Orioles On SI sites, and additionally contributes to Athlon Sports and Men’s Journal covering Major League Baseball and other trending sports news. Joe is a graduate of Rutgers University in 2022, earning a bachelor’s degree in Journalism and Media Studies.

item.title: [Empire Sports Media] NY Yankees' bargain bat is worth another year, not a bigger role
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson

item.content:encoded:
Paul Goldschmidt wants to keep playing. The Yankees should consider giving him another year, provided they aren’t buying back an everyday first baseman.
Ben Rice earned that job. A reunion would make sense as a way to strengthen the bench against left-handed pitching, not as an excuse to reduce Rice’s role after a 41-homer season.
“I’d like to continue playing, so we’ll see if that opportunity happens,” Goldschmidt told Newsday’s Roger Rubin after New York’s elimination. He played this season on a one-year, $4 million contract. There is no established offer or price for a 2027 return.
The Yankees have a very specific use for Goldschmidt
Goldschmidt hit .299/.393/.573 against lefties, with 11 home runs in 183 plate appearances. Against righties, he dropped to .213/.239/.351 in 197 plate appearances. A .966 OPS on one side and .590 on the other is a pretty good argument for being selective about when he plays.
The full-season line was respectable: .252/.313/.452, 18 home runs and 52 RBIs in 105 games. But treating those numbers as an argument for regular starts would miss the important part. His best contribution came against a particular group of pitchers.
Rice hit .264/.363/.534 with 41 homers in 154 games. New York needs to build around that production. Goldschmidt shouldn’t automatically start whenever an opponent uses a left-handed pitcher, either. Rice still needs opportunities to face them, and the manager has to consider the specific matchup rather than the handedness alone.
I like the idea of keeping Goldschmidt for selected starts and late-game pinch-hitting opportunities. I don’t like the idea of signing him first and figuring out how to divide the at-bats afterward. The role should be clear before the contract is.
A bench spot has to justify the restrictions
Goldschmidt is 39. A one-year commitment would reduce the risk of a longer decline, but it wouldn’t remove it. Those platoon samples are also fewer than 200 plate appearances each. New York can’t assume he will repeat either split exactly.
There is a reasonable alternative: use the opening on a right-handed hitter who can cover more positions. Goldschmidt’s offense against lefties would have to be valuable enough to justify a narrower defensive role. Familiarity isn’t a substitute for that comparison.
The price matters, too. His $4 million salary describes the season that just ended, not a discount already available for next year. If the cost rises substantially, or he wants a larger role, the Yankees should be comfortable passing.
Bringing him back doesn’t have to mean blocking Rice. It would mean using a veteran for the work he still does well and accepting the limitations elsewhere. Give Goldschmidt a short deal and a defined assignment if the terms fit. Keep Rice’s everyday role intact.

item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday night, the New York Yankees lost to the Tampa Bay Rays by a score of 4-3 in the Bronx.
With the loss, the Yankees got swept in the ALDS (in three games).
ESPN’s Jeff Passan wrote: “The best team in the league finishes the sweep and heads to the ALCS. A game-tying Anthony Volpe home run was overturned because of fan interference, and the Rays held their one-run lead for the final 10 outs. The Yankees haven’t won a title in 17 years.”
Alex Rodriguez Was Right About Failed Yankees Star
One of the biggest reasons for their loss was the play of Trent Grisham.
He finished with no hits and three strikeouts in five at-bats.
Grisham’s failure this season has been a hot topic among Yankees fans.
Trent Grisham #12 of the New York Yankees bats against the Tampa Bay Rays during the third inning in game three of the American League Division Series at Yankee Stadium on October 07, 2026 in the Bronx borough of New York City.
With Grisham failing in their most important game of the season, it’s worth noting that Alex Rodriguez made intriguing comments on August 11 (via The Michael Kay Show).
Kay: “Are you stunned, Alex, by how much the Yankee offense has been affected because Judge is out?”
Rodriguez: “I’m not that surprised, Michael… Obviously I’m an enormous Yankee fan and I watch a lot. I thought the party started when they got Grisham and I heard your show almost every day. I saw how angry the fans got for the $22 million and I heard you say that maybe the proper number would have been three for 15 or three for 25 or three for 30, which probably would have been a lot more appropriate. But it’s amazing how the whole fan base knew exactly how this was going to turn out and it did.”
Looking At Grisham
Trent Grisham #12 of the New York Yankees is walked during the fifth inning against the Minnesota Twins at Yankee Stadium on July 04, 2026 in New York City.
Grisham finished his third season with the Yankees batting .211 with 18 home runs, 59 RBIs, 67 runs and nine stolen bases in 121 games.
He has also spent time with the Milwaukee Brewers and San Diego Padres over eight years.

item.title: [New York Post] Anthony Volpe’s strong end to year gives him another chance at a Yankees future
item.dc:creator: Greg Joyce
item.description:
In a season full of swings, Anthony Volpe nearly saved his best for last. Alas, what initially looked like a game-tying, two-run homer in Game 3 of the ALDS could not be saved by the second coming of Jeffrey Maier, and a few innings later, the Yankees were swept by the Rays.

item.content:encoded:
In a season full of swings, Anthony Volpe nearly saved his best for last.
Alas, what initially looked like a game-tying, two-run homer in Game 3 of the ALDS could not be saved by the second coming of Jeffrey Maier, and a few innings later, the Yankees were swept by the Rays.




Access the Yankees beat like never before

Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
But Volpe’s near-moment, after a season in which he was twice demoted to Triple-A after losing his job as the Yankees starting shortstop, was a reminder that he may still have a place in the future of the organization, namely as their second baseman next season.
There is a long way to go between now and whenever (or if) baseball begins in 2027 — due to the looming lockout — but as the Yankees enter the offseason, Volpe has at least given himself a chance to find a home again in pinstripes, as George Lombard Jr.’s double-play partner.
“If we were going to go win a World Series, we needed Anthony Volpe on the team,” Aaron Judge said late Wednesday night. “He’s an incredible player, not only the talent he has, but to handle that type of adversity — not only from the game, not playing your best and then hearing it from fans, hearing it from everybody, and then for him to go down to Triple-A, work on what he needed to and then come up here with a bang like he did, it speaks volumes to his character and the type of grit he has.”
It was not long ago that Volpe was at Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre, looking like a player who might benefit from a change of scenery in a trade this offseason. It is not out of the question that the 25-year-old could still be dealt this winter, depending on how the Yankees offseason shakes out. But with Jazz Chisholm Jr. headed to free agency and unlikely to return (despite his wishes), Volpe at the very least looks like a placeholder at second base, if not something more.
In the Yankees’ five playoff games, Volpe started over Chisholm twice. The first came against Red Sox lefty Payton Tolle in Game 1 of the AL wild-card series before Chisholm’s untrustworthiness led to Volpe starting again in Game 3 of the ALDS against Rays righty Nick Martinez with the season on the line.
Aaron Boone even considered starting Volpe at third base, a position at which he has played just one career major league game, for Game 2 against the Rays before deciding not to risk his first game there on Tropicana Field’s turf coming in the playoffs (though the decision to stick with Ryan McMahon still ultimately burned the Yankees).
That Volpe was at second base for Game 3 was an indictment of Chisholm, but it also spoke to how the club believes in Volpe’s makeup, which was reinforced with how he responded to the demotion to Triple-A when he was replaced by Lombard after the trade deadline.
“Volpe, what he’s able to do, talk about facing adversity, and what’s it tell you about him and his character and his makeup and his ability?” Boone said. “The way he’s come back and the level of at-bats he’s throwing up there [in Game 3], getting off the mat.”
While Volpe hit 3-for-7 with a double and two strikeouts in his two playoff games this year, it remains a question what the Yankees could get out of him offensively next season. The demotion to Triple-A gave him the time to make some adjustments in his swing — ones he couldn’t fully make last offseason, which he spent most of rehabbing shoulder surgery — most notably using a stepback with his back foot to get him in a better rhythm.
In the 14 regular-season games he played after coming back up from Triple-A, he hit .265 with a .695 OPS, one home run and five steals. Whether there is more where that came from (meaning more than his career .661 OPS across four seasons) remains to be seen.
Volpe did look comfortable at second base, where his arm plays better and gives him more time to not have to rush plays, and it might just be his ticket to staying in The Bronx next year after a turbulent season.
“I just wanted to stay in the moment,” Volpe said late Wednesday night. “I haven’t really even gotten to think of what’s happened or what happened to me or this year, anything like that, or how to get better from it. I just always tried to stay in the moment and do what I could do every single day to make myself the best player I can be, the best teammate, the best Yankee, everything.”

item.content:encoded:
Good morning! The NBA season is around the corner, and Portland Trail Blazers forward Deni Avdija is already reminding fans why he became the NBA’s first Israeli All-Star last season.
Avdija dropped a team-high 23 points in his preseason debut on Wednesday, with two rebounds and two assists in just 21 minutes.
The season tips off on Oct. 20.
Max Fried’s very bittersweet week
New York Yankees ace Max Fried took the mound Wednesday as the Bronx Bombers looked to stave off elimination against the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
It didn’t work.
The Yankees lost, 4-3, and were swept by their division rivals. Despite the low-scoring games, the series was never particularly close. Fried allowed four runs — including two home runs — in 5 2/3 innings, while the Yankees’ offense remained quiet. (Rowdy Tellez and the Atlanta Braves were also eliminated on Wednesday.) 
It’s another unfortunate chapter in Fried’s postseason career. His 5.11 career ERA in the playoffs is the worst in MLB history among pitchers with 75+ innings pitched.
But there’s a silver lining for Fried, who is set to become a father any day now.
Fried, who is typically on the private side when it comes to his personal life, confirmed before the game that his girlfriend, the former University of Southern California volleyball star Reni Meyer-Whalley, was due to give birth to the couple’s first child this week.
“I’d not like to get too into the personal stuff, but yeah, that’s true,” Fried said on Tuesday when asked about the pregnancy.
“I’ve got a real supportive family that understands that this is my job,” he added. “And it’s not going to affect what happens tomorrow.”
So the Yankees may be eliminated, but at least Fried will have a happy distraction this offseason. Mazel tov!
Halftime report
WE MEET AGAIN. Israel and Ireland played their second soccer match in as many weeks last Sunday, and it was just as tense as the first one. Irish players again wore black armbands, declined handshakes and bowed their heads during the Israeli national anthem. This time, the drama spilled off the pitch, too, with Israeli journalists clashing with Ireland’s football association at a heated press conference. Here’s more.
VOTE EARLY AND OFTEN. As the year draws to a close, the International Jewish Sports Hall of Fame is holding a fan vote for the Jewish athletes and performances of the year — from Deni Avdija’s breakout season and Jack Hughes’ heroics at the Olympics to Amit Elor and Jessica Fox’s dominance on the international stage. Cast your votes right here.
WELCOME BACK. Former college basketball star Dan Grunfeld is returning to his alma mater, Stanford University, as the men’s basketball team’s new general manager and assistant coach. After leading Stanford to three NCAA tournaments (including as a No. 1 seed in 2004), Grunfeld played in the NBA Summer League and abroad in Germany, Spain and Israel. He is the son of former NBA player and general manager Ernie Grunfeld, the only known child of Holocaust survivors to play in the league. Dan chronicles his family’s story in his book, “By the Grace of the Game: The Holocaust, a Basketball Legacy, and an Unprecedented American Dream.”

item.content:encoded:
This would be very interesting.
However, now that the postseason has ended, the Yankees will have a lot to consider. Jazz Chisholm Jr. is a very good player in his own right, but there are many concerns about bringing him back to the Yankees.
The Yankees have to ensure they put themselves in a good position payroll-wise, and giving Chisholm as much money as he's likely looking for doesn't help. While the Yankees can definitely spend more money, that doesn't mean they should hand out contracts they don't want to.
If the Yankees want to move on from Chisholm, a few obvious candidates could take over at second base.
Youngster Anthony Volpe would be at the top of that list, though it remains uncertain what the Yankees want to do with him, too. Volpe was great in the postseason and deserves a lot of credit.
As for other guys who could fit nicely with what the Yankees are trying to do, perhaps a guy like Luis Garcia could move back to second. Garcia has some experience playing up the middle throughout his Major League Baseball career, despite playing first base in New York.
Still only 26 years old, Garcia was recently floated as a potential option.
“The Nationals moved García to first base this year, which worked out well. He has 2 DRS, 3 OAA and 2 FRV so far at his new position. At the plate, he has had the best season of his career. Whether the defensive switch helped him focus on his hitting is something that could be debated but the end result was García hitting 30 home runs, almost doubling his previous high of 18. He slashed .277/.309/.521 for a 124 wRC+. In previous seasons, he only once had a wRC+ above 95, posting a 108 in 2024.
“García can be retained for one more year via arbitration. Given his offensive performance, it would make sense for the Yanks to bring him back. MLBTR contributor Matt Swartz projects García for a salary of $11MM next year,” Darragh McDonald of MLBTR wrote.
Garcia isn't the typical middle infielder's size, but he can swing it with the best of them offensively, and he needs to be in the Yankees' lineup day in and day out.
He's one of the better trade deadline additions the Yankees have made in quite some time, and if they want to get creative at first base next season, this lets them do so.
It's not a big deal right now, but it could make sense for the Yankees over the next year.
